questions.stem:
An engineer argues: "Last month, the factory's defect rate fell sharply. Either the new quality-control checklist caused the drop, the milder weather reduced humidity-related warping, or the reassignment of the night-shift supervisor improved oversight. We can rule out the weather: temperature and humidity logs show conditions nearly identical to the prior month. We can also rule out the supervisor reassignment: the new supervisor wasn't scheduled to start until three weeks after the drop had already leveled off. So the checklist must be responsible."

The engineer's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: inferring that the checklist caused the drop merely because the two events happened to occur around the same time, without considering whether other factors might explain the timing

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing a general rule about defect rates from a single factory's experience and applying that rule to the manufacturing industry as a whole

choices.label: C
choices.text: presuming, without independent proof, that quality-control checklists are inherently effective, and using that presumption to account for the data

choices.label: D
choices.text: eliminating two competing explanations for the observed drop by citing independent evidence against each, leaving the remaining explanation as the best-supported one

choices.label: E
choices.text: comparing the factory's situation to an analogous case at a different plant where a checklist also coincided with a reduction in defects

questions.explanation: D is correct: the engineer considers three candidate explanations, rules out two of them using independent evidence (matching weather logs; a supervisor start date after the drop had leveled off), and concludes that the surviving explanation is responsible — the classic method of eliminating alternatives. A is wrong because the engineer does not rely on mere timing; the argument explicitly rules out the two other candidates using evidence unrelated to timing, rather than inferring causation from correlation alone. B is wrong because no general industry-wide rule is drawn or applied; the conclusion is limited to this factory's defect rate. C is wrong because the engineer never simply presumes checklists work; the conclusion rests on ruling out rivals, not on an unproven assumption about checklists in general. E is wrong because no other plant or analogous case is mentioned anywhere in the argument.

questions.stem:
Historians know that a town's founding date is best established by contemporaneous written records. The earliest surviving municipal document that mentions the town of Millbrook is dated 1841, and no surviving document assigns Millbrook an earlier founding date. Historians have therefore concluded that Millbrook was founded in 1841.

Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historians' reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Millbrook's 1841 municipal document is the oldest surviving document of its kind in the entire region.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most towns founded before 1841 have surviving records of their founding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Millbrook's municipal records from 1841 onward are completely accurate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Written records are the only reliable evidence of a town's founding date.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If Millbrook had been founded before 1841, some written record of that founding would have survived to the present.

questions.explanation: The historians infer 'founded in 1841' from 'no surviving document says earlier,' which is an appeal to absent evidence. That inference holds only if an earlier founding would have left a surviving trace. Negate E - suppose Millbrook could have been founded earlier without any record surviving - and the absence of an earlier-dated document proves nothing, so E is required. A compares Millbrook's document to other regional documents, which is irrelevant to Millbrook's own founding date. B speaks only to a general statistical tendency across other towns and doesn't establish what would have happened in Millbrook's specific case, so it's the wrong scope to do the needed work. C concerns the accuracy of later records, not whether any record of an earlier founding would exist, so it's out of scope. D overshoots: the argument doesn't need written records to be the only reliable evidence in general, only that an earlier founding of Millbrook specifically would have produced a surviving one.

D is a generalization neither speaker states. E is mentioned by neither.

questions.stem:
Restoring the wetland would cost the county nine million dollars. But the wetland absorbs runoff that the county's storm drains would otherwise have to carry, and expanding the drain system to that capacity would cost fourteen million. So the restoration pays for itself. The county should therefore fund it in this budget cycle rather than deferring it again.

The claim that the restoration pays for itself plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the argument's main conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise offered without support.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a conclusion drawn from a cost comparison and offered in support of a further conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a consideration the argument concedes before rejecting it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background information that plays no role in the reasoning.

questions.explanation: Run the two-way test. What supports 'the restoration pays for itself'? The nine-versus-fourteen million comparison. What does it support? The recommendation to fund it now. Supported and supporting: an intermediate conclusion — C. A names the wrong tier; the main conclusion is the final sentence's recommendation. B is wrong because the cost comparison is exactly its support. D describes a concession, but nothing here is granted and then rejected. E is contradicted by the 'so' that introduces it.

questions.stem:
A four-year study of a court's mandatory mediation program found that mediated cases settled at nearly the same rate as unmediated ones, but that mediated cases which settled did so an average of five months earlier. Mediated cases that did not settle went to trial no later than comparable unmediated cases.

The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory mediation causes cases to settle that would not otherwise have settled.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mediation program should be adopted by every court in the jurisdiction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The program's principal effect is on the timing of settlements rather than on how many cases settle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cases that go to trial after mediation are resolved more quickly than those that go to trial without it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Litigants who participate in mediation are more satisfied with the outcome than those who do not.

questions.explanation: Settlement rates were 'nearly the same' while settled cases resolved five months earlier, and non-settling cases were not delayed. The claim the findings best support is that the program moves timing, not volume — C, and note how modestly it is worded. A is contradicted by the equal settlement rates. B is a recommendation the data alone cannot license, and 'every court' overreaches. D reverses the third finding, which says trial timing was *no later*, not earlier. E introduces satisfaction, which the study never measured.

questions.stem:
Every associate who bills more than two thousand hours receives the annual bonus. No associate in the pro bono rotation receives the annual bonus. At least one associate in the pro bono rotation was promoted this year.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some associates who bill more than two thousand hours were not promoted this year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No associate in the pro bono rotation bills more than two thousand hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some associates who received the annual bonus were not promoted this year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every associate who was promoted this year bills more than two thousand hours.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every associate outside the pro bono rotation received the annual bonus.

questions.explanation: Chain the first two statements: billing over two thousand hours guarantees the bonus, and rotation members never get the bonus, so by contrapositive no rotation member bills over two thousand hours. The third statement puts at least one rotation member among this year's promotions. D says every promoted associate bills over two thousand — but that promoted rotation member does not, so D collides with the derived inference and cannot be true. B is the trap: it states the derived inference itself, so far from being impossible it MUST be true. A, C, and E are each consistent — nothing links billing or the bonus to promotion in either direction, and nothing bars the firm from paying the bonus to everyone outside the rotation.

questions.stem:
Two years ago the hospital introduced a checklist that surgical teams must complete before every operation. Since then, the rate of post-operative infection has fallen by a third. The checklist is therefore responsible for the decline.

Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: How long it takes a surgical team to complete the checklist

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether the hospital adopted any other infection-control measure during the same two years

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether other hospitals in the region have adopted similar checklists

choices.label: D
choices.text: What the post-operative infection rate was three years before the checklist was introduced

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether surgical teams find the checklist burdensome

questions.explanation: Apply the variance test. If the hospital adopted no other measure, the checklist's claim to credit is much stronger; if it also, say, changed its sterilization protocol, an alternative cause is live and the argument weakens. B swings the argument both ways. A and E bear on cost and morale, not on whether the checklist caused the decline. C tells us about other hospitals' choices, which leaves this hospital's causal story untouched. D is tempting — a trend already falling would weaken — but a single earlier figure establishes no trend, so either answer leaves the argument roughly where it was.

questions.stem:
Every witness who testified at the hearing was placed under oath. Okonkwo did not testify at the hearing. It does not follow that Okonkwo was not placed under oath, because ___

Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: some witnesses who testify are not credible

choices.label: B
choices.text: people other than testifying witnesses are sometimes placed under oath

choices.label: C
choices.text: Okonkwo was present at the hearing

choices.label: D
choices.text: the hearing officer has discretion over who testifies

choices.label: E
choices.text: not every person placed under oath tells the truth

questions.explanation: The connector is 'because', so the blank wants the premise that licenses the stated conclusion. The argument says the inference fails — and it fails precisely because 'all testifying witnesses were sworn' leaves open that non-witnesses were sworn too. B supplies exactly that. A and E are about credibility and truthfulness, which the argument never touches. C is topical but does nothing: being present neither implies nor excludes being sworn. D explains who testifies, not who is sworn.

questions.stem:
Last year the public defender's office resolved a smaller percentage of its cases by plea than it did a decade ago. Clearly, then, fewer of the office's clients are pleading guilty than a decade ago.

The reasoning above is most vulnerable to criticism on the ground that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that a decline in a proportion establishes a decline in an absolute number

choices.label: B
choices.text: confuses a claim about the public defender's office with a claim about defence counsel generally

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes without warrant that pleading guilty is undesirable

choices.label: D
choices.text: relies on a sample of cases too small to support a general conclusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a correlation between two trends as though it established a causal link

questions.explanation: The premise is a share ('a smaller percentage'); the conclusion is a count ('fewer clients'). Both can be true only if the caseload did not grow — and if it grew enough, a smaller share is a larger number. A names the switch. B alleges a scope shift the argument does not make; it stays with one office throughout. C imports an evaluative assumption the argument never needs. D complains about sample size, but the argument reports the office's own caseload rather than sampling it. E describes a causal flaw in an argument that draws no causal conclusion.

questions.stem:
The bar association mailed a survey to all of its members asking whether the continuing-education requirement should be increased. Of the members who returned the survey, sixty-two percent said it should. The association concluded that most of its members favour an increase.

The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: fails to consider that members might change their views over time

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats members who returned the survey as representative of members generally, though members with strong views about the requirement are likelier to have responded

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a policy from evidence about opinions

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from a sample that is too small to be reliable

choices.label: E
choices.text: assumes that what most members favour is what the association should do

questions.explanation: The sample selected itself: only members who chose to return the survey are counted, and an opinion question about a burdensome requirement is exactly the kind that motivates the strongly-opinionated to respond. B names the mismatch between how the sample was assembled and the population concluded about. A raises a timing worry the argument does not depend on. C misdescribes the conclusion, which is about member opinion, not about policy. D reaches for sample size — the tempting wrong answer here, since nothing tells us the response count was small, and size was never the defect. E attacks a normative step the argument never takes.

questions.stem:
Critics who dismiss the novel as sentimental have simply failed to read it with the attention it deserves. We know this because anyone who reads the novel attentively comes to recognize that its emotional directness is a deliberate technique rather than a lapse in craft — and no one who recognizes that would call the book sentimental.

The reasoning above is most vulnerable to criticism on the ground that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes a claim to be false merely because those who assert it are unqualified

choices.label: B
choices.text: presupposes what it purports to establish, by defining attentive reading as reading that reaches the author's own verdict

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all critics from evidence about some of them

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses a sufficient condition for attentive reading with a necessary one

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on an appeal to the authority of readers who share the author's view

questions.explanation: The conclusion is that dismissive critics read inattentively. The support is that attentive readers all reach the opposite verdict — which is true only because the argument has built the verdict into what 'attentive' means. Accepting the premise requires already accepting the conclusion: B. A describes an ad hominem, and the argument attacks the reading rather than the reader's standing. C alleges hasty generalization, but the claim covers exactly the critics the premise is about. D names a conditional confusion the argument does not commit — its conditional runs one direction throughout. E is close in flavour and wrong in mechanism: no authority is invoked; the circle is definitional.

questions.stem:
Ferreira: Requiring judicial nominees to answer questions about specific pending controversies would compromise their impartiality. A nominee who has publicly committed to a view cannot later decide the matter with an open mind.

Wong: Nominees already have views; the hearing only reveals them. What compromises impartiality is deciding a case one has prejudged, and that risk exists whether or not the prejudgment was ever spoken aloud.

Ferreira and Wong disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: judicial nominees typically hold views about pending controversies

choices.label: B
choices.text: publicly stating a view about a controversy makes a nominee less able to decide it impartially than holding that view privately does

choices.label: C
choices.text: impartiality is a desirable quality in a judge

choices.label: D
choices.text: confirmation hearings serve any useful purpose

choices.label: E
choices.text: a judge who has prejudged a case should recuse from it

questions.explanation: Ferreira's argument turns on the *public commitment* doing the damage; Wong's reply is that the damage is done by the prejudgment itself, so speaking it aloud adds nothing. That comparative claim is the disagreement — B. A is Wong's premise and Ferreira does not deny it; indeed Ferreira's worry presupposes nominees can form views. C is common ground. D is never addressed by Ferreira. E is a remedy neither speaker discusses, which is what makes it a clean failure of the two-part test.

questions.stem:
An insurer analyzed two of its regional call centres. At the Northern centre, claims handlers who completed the optional fraud-detection training referred four percent of claims for investigation; handlers who did not complete it referred two percent. At the Southern centre the same gap appeared. The insurer concluded that the training makes handlers better at detecting fraud, and it made the training mandatory company-wide.

Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the insurer's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: What proportion of referred claims were ultimately confirmed to be fraudulent, among handlers who had completed the training and among those who had not

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether the two regional centres handle claims of comparable value

choices.label: C
choices.text: How many handlers at each centre completed the optional training

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether handlers who completed the training had been employed longer than those who had not

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether the company-wide mandatory training uses the same curriculum as the optional version

questions.explanation: The conclusion is about *detection* — finding fraud — but every figure in the stimulus is a referral rate, which measures suspicion, not accuracy. A goes straight to that gap: if trained handlers' referrals are confirmed as fraud at the same or a higher rate, the training is detecting better; if their extra referrals are overwhelmingly unfounded, the training merely made them refer more. Both answers move the argument decisively. D is the strong distractor — it supplies an alternative cause, self-selection by tenure — but it is second best, because even a perfect answer leaves the referral-versus-detection gap untouched: longer-tenured handlers referring more still tells us nothing about whether those referrals were right. B and C bear on comparability and sample size without touching the inference from referrals to detection. E concerns the remedy the insurer adopted rather than the conclusion it drew.

questions.stem:
Council member: The protected bike lane on Third Street will slow the buses that share the corridor, and riders on those routes will feel it. But the delay is smaller than the one drivers already impose on the buses by double-parking, and the lane will pull cyclists out of the bus lane, where they slow buses most. The lane should be built this year.

The claim that the bike lane will slow the buses that share the corridor plays which one of the following roles in the council member's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion the council member argues for.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is evidence offered in direct support of the recommendation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a claim the council member argues is false.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a cost the council member grants and then argues is outweighed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an assumption required for the recommendation to follow.

questions.explanation: The sentence is introduced as a real drawback and is immediately met with 'But' — the mark of a concession the arguer accepts and then answers. D says exactly that. A misreads the tier: the conclusion is the last sentence's recommendation. B has the support running the wrong way; a cost of building the lane cannot be evidence for building it. C is wrong because the council member never disputes that buses will be slowed, only that the delay is decisive. E confuses a conceded objection with a required premise; the argument would be stronger, not broken, if the delay did not exist.

questions.stem:
In one state's small-claims court, litigants may appear with or without a lawyer. Cases in which neither side has a lawyer are resolved, on average, in half the time of cases in which at least one side does. When one side has a lawyer and the other does not, the represented side prevails substantially more often than the unrepresented side. When both sides have lawyers, neither side prevails more often than the other.

The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A litigant in this court who hires a lawyer is more likely to prevail than one who does not, whatever the opposing side does.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether hiring a lawyer improves a litigant's chances in this court depends on whether the opposing side also has one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cases resolved quickly in this court are more likely to be decided correctly than cases resolved slowly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most litigants who appear in this court appear without a lawyer.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lawyers lengthen proceedings in this court by raising issues the court would not otherwise have to resolve.

questions.explanation: Put the two outcome facts side by side: a lawyer against an unrepresented opponent wins substantially more often, and a lawyer against another lawyer wins no more often. The advantage therefore turns on what the other side does, which is B. A overstates it into a claim the third fact directly contradicts. C rates accuracy, which the stimulus never measures. D is about how common representation is; the stimulus gives averages, not proportions of litigants. E converts a reported association between representation and duration into a causal mechanism the facts do not establish.

questions.stem:
Every grant application the ethics panel reviews is either funded or returned for revision. No application returned for revision is reviewed again in the same funding cycle. An application submitted after March 1 is reviewed by the panel only if a director sponsors it. Every sponsored application is funded.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An application submitted before March 1 was returned for revision.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An application was funded although no director sponsored it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A director sponsored an application that was submitted before March 1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An application submitted after March 1 was reviewed by the panel and returned for revision.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An application returned for revision in one funding cycle was reviewed in a later cycle.

questions.explanation: Chain the last two conditions. Reviewed and submitted after March 1 means sponsored; sponsored means funded; and funded rules out returned for revision, since the first sentence makes the two outcomes exclusive. D asserts all of that at once, so D cannot be true. A and C concern applications the March 1 rule never reaches. B is consistent: sponsorship guarantees funding but is nowhere made necessary for it. E is barred only within the same cycle, and E moves to a later one.

questions.stem:
Digitizing a court's paper files reduces the time clerks spend retrieving records, but it does not by itself reduce the court's backlog. The backlog forms at the hearing stage, where the number of judges available to hear matters, and not the speed with which files reach them, sets the pace at which cases clear. So a court that digitizes its files without adding judges should expect ______

Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: its backlog to fall roughly in proportion to the time its clerks save.

choices.label: B
choices.text: its backlog to grow more quickly than it did before digitization.

choices.label: C
choices.text: its clerks' retrieval work to fall while its backlog stays roughly where it was.

choices.label: D
choices.text: its clerks to spend more time retrieving records than they did before.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the number of judges available to hear matters to fall.

questions.explanation: The passage grants one effect and denies another: retrieval time drops, the backlog does not, because judges rather than files are the bottleneck. C is that pair of results and nothing more, so C completes the argument. A asserts the very drop the second sentence rules out. B goes further still, predicting a worsening the passage gives no reason to expect. D contradicts the first sentence. E introduces a change in judicial staffing that the passage neither states nor implies.

questions.stem:
The number of appeals filed in this state's intermediate appellate court rose by thirty percent over the last decade. Appellate work must therefore make up a larger share of the state's legal practice than it did ten years ago.

The reasoning above is most vulnerable to criticism on the ground that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes without warrant that the additional appeals filed were meritorious

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats an increase in appeals filed as though it were an increase in appeals decided

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a period longer than the one its evidence covers

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that the rise in filings was caused by an increase in errors at trial

choices.label: E
choices.text: infers a change in a proportion from a change in an absolute number, with no information about the total

questions.explanation: The evidence is a count of appeals; the conclusion is appellate work's share of all legal practice. If every other kind of legal work grew by thirty percent as well, the share is unchanged, and if the rest grew faster, the share fell. E names that missing denominator. A and D attack quality and cause, neither of which the conclusion is about. B alleges a filed-versus-decided switch, but the conclusion concerns work performed, which filings do measure. C is false on the face of it: evidence and conclusion cover the same decade.

questions.stem:
To gauge local opinion on the new zoning ordinance, a newspaper invited readers to submit comments through its website. Of the four hundred comments received, three hundred forty opposed the ordinance. The newspaper reported that most residents of the town oppose it.

The newspaper's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about residents' opinions from evidence about the ordinance's merits

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider that a single reader may have submitted more than one comment

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats people who chose to respond as though they represented the population as a whole

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that opposition to a zoning ordinance shows the ordinance to be unwise

choices.label: E
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that opinion will shift once the ordinance takes effect

questions.explanation: Nobody selected these respondents but themselves, and the residents most moved to write are the residents who object. A self-selected sample cannot support a claim about everyone, which is C. B names a real hygiene problem with web comments, but even one comment per person leaves the sample self-selected, so it is not what breaks the inference. A misdescribes the evidence, which is opinion rather than merit. D and E answer questions the newspaper never asked: whether the ordinance is wise, and what residents will think later.

questions.stem:
Attorney: My client's account of the accident is credible. He would never lie under oath, as we know from the fact that he is a credible witness.

The reasoning in the attorney's argument is flawed in that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on the testimony of someone with an interest in the outcome

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a condition that is necessary for credibility as though it were sufficient

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes about all of the client's statements from a single one

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes the truth of the very claim it is supposed to establish

choices.label: E
choices.text: criticizes those who doubt the client instead of answering their reasons

questions.explanation: The conclusion is that the client is credible; the support offered is that he would not lie under oath; the support for that is that he is credible. The chain returns to its starting point, which is D. B describes a conditional confusion, but nothing here is offered as a necessary condition. A is a fair observation about interested witnesses and no part of this argument's structure. C invents a generalization the attorney never makes. E describes an ad hominem, and the attorney attacks no one.

questions.stem:
Every witness who testified on Monday was cross-examined. Ruiz testified on Monday.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ruiz testified only on Monday.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every witness who was cross-examined testified on Monday.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some witnesses who testified on Monday were not cross-examined.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ruiz was the only witness cross-examined on Monday.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ruiz was cross-examined.

questions.explanation: The first sentence is a conditional — testified Monday, therefore cross-examined — and the second supplies the condition for Ruiz. E follows and nothing more does. B reverses the conditional, which is not an inference the premises license. C contradicts the first sentence outright. A and D add exclusivity claims — only Monday, only Ruiz — that the premises never mention.

questions.stem:
The city's recycling program costs more per tonne than sending the same waste to a landfill. But the landfill will reach capacity in six years, and the nearest alternative site is ninety kilometres away. The city should keep funding the recycling program.

Which one of the following is the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city should keep funding the recycling program.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The recycling program costs more per tonne than landfilling.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The landfill will reach capacity within six years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nearest alternative landfill site is ninety kilometres away.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recycling will become cheaper than landfilling within six years.

questions.explanation: The last sentence is the recommendation everything else is offered to support, which makes A the main conclusion. B is the cost fact the argument concedes, and C and D are the two considerations offered against it. E is a prediction the argument never makes; it claims the landfill will fill up, not that recycling will become the cheaper option.

questions.stem:
The clinic's new intake form is shorter than the old one. Clients will therefore complete it more quickly.

The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The old intake form was longer than any other form the clinic uses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clients who complete the form quickly are more likely to return.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The clinic's staff prefer the new intake form to the old one.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The new form's questions are not harder to answer than the old form's.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No client will need help completing the new form.

questions.explanation: Shorter does not mean faster if the remaining questions are harder to answer; the argument needs that possibility ruled out, which is D. Negate it and the conclusion collapses. A compares the old form with other forms, which the argument never does. B adds a benefit of speed the conclusion does not claim. C reports a preference the argument does not rely on. E is far stronger than the argument needs: some clients could need help and the form could still be quicker on average.

questions.stem:
After the library began opening on Sundays, weekly visits rose by a fifth. The Sunday hours must be what drew the additional visitors.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The library's Sunday staff are the same people who work on Saturdays.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most libraries in the region are closed on Sundays.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A new bus route serving the library opened in the same week as the Sunday hours.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Visits on Saturdays fell slightly after the Sunday hours began.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The library's collection has not grown since the Sunday hours began.

questions.explanation: The argument treats the Sunday hours as the cause of the rise. C supplies a rival cause that arrived at exactly the same time, which is the standard way a causal claim of this shape is undermined. D is the tempting answer, but a small fall on Saturdays is consistent with a fifth more visits overall and does nothing to explain where the extra visitors came from. A and E report facts that leave the causal question untouched, and B, if anything, helps the argument by making the library unusual in the region.

questions.stem:
Critic: A restoration is faithful only if it uses the materials the original artisans used. The chapel's roof was restored with modern tiles, so the restoration is not faithful — and since the trust funds only faithful restorations, it will not fund this one.

Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A dish is authentic only if it is cooked in a clay pot. This stew was cooked in a clay pot, so it is authentic, and the guide lists only authentic dishes, so it will list this stew.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A grant is renewable only if the project reports on time. This project reported late, so its grant is not renewable — and since the board renews only renewable grants, it will not renew this one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A translation is accurate only if the translator knows both languages. This translator knows both languages, so the translation may well be accurate, and the press publishes translations that may well be accurate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A building is historic only if it is more than a century old. The annex is ninety years old, so it is not historic, and the registry lists most historic buildings, so it probably will not list the annex.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A claim is admissible only if it is filed within a year. This claim was filed within a year, so it is admissible, and the tribunal hears only admissible claims, so it will hear this one.

questions.explanation: The original runs: X only if Y; not Y; so not X; and since only X gets the benefit, this one does not. Two moves, both valid — denying the necessary condition, then applying a second necessary condition to withhold the benefit. B repeats both exactly. A and E instead affirm the necessary condition and conclude the thing holds, which is the invalid converse and so a different pattern, valid or not. C weakens every step to a possibility and reaches no comparable conclusion. D matches the first move but softens the second into 'most' and 'probably', so the conclusion no longer follows as it does in the original.

questions.stem:
Principle: A public body may withhold a document only if releasing it would harm an interest the body is charged with protecting, and only if that harm outweighs the public's interest in seeing the document.

Which one of the following judgements most closely conforms to the principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A housing agency withholds a contractor's bid because releasing it would embarrass the contractor, whose reputation the agency has no duty to protect, and because the public interest in the bid is slight.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A police service releases an informant's name because the public interest in the case is intense, although disclosure would put the informant at serious risk of harm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A health authority withholds a hospital's inspection report because releasing it would undermine public confidence in the hospital, an interest the authority protects, even though the report bears directly on patient safety.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A water utility withholds a map of its pipe network because releasing it would help vandals disable the supply, which the utility is charged with protecting, and the public can see the same safety data in the utility's annual report.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A school board releases a teacher's disciplinary file because the board's policy is to release all personnel records on request.

questions.explanation: The principle permits withholding only when both tests are met: a protected interest is harmed, and that harm outweighs the public's interest in the document. D is the only judgement that satisfies both — the utility's charge is the supply itself, and the public interest is slight because the same safety information is published elsewhere. A fails the first test, since the agency protects no interest in the contractor's reputation. C is the near miss: the interest is protected but a report bearing directly on patient safety is exactly where the public interest is weightiest, so the balance goes the other way. B and E concern releases, and the principle constrains only withholding — neither judgement can conform to it or violate it.

questions.stem:
Editor: Every article we publish is fact-checked. An article is published only if two editors have approved it. Kovac approved the article on the bridge collapse, and it was fact-checked. So it will be published.

The reasoning above is most vulnerable to criticism on the ground that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats the fact that every published article is fact-checked as though fact-checking guaranteed publication, and treats one editor's approval as though it were two

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes without warrant that Kovac is an editor whose approval counts

choices.label: C
choices.text: confuses a claim about the editor's own articles with a claim about every article the publication runs

choices.label: D
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that an article could be fact-checked after it is published rather than before

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that the second editor's approval might be withdrawn before publication

questions.explanation: Two distinct errors, and the credited answer has to name both. Fact-checking is stated as a *consequence* of publication, not a condition for it, so 'it was fact-checked' supports nothing; and two approvals are necessary, so one approval does not supply even the condition that is required. A is the only option that reports both. B raises a question the stimulus settles by calling Kovac an approver in an editor's own argument. D and E invent timing and withdrawal scenarios that leave the two structural errors untouched, and E in particular presupposes a second approval the stimulus never reports. C describes a scope shift the argument does not make.

questions.stem:
Two towns drew their drinking water from the same aquifer. After the eastern town installed a filtration plant, reported cases of gastrointestinal illness there fell by a third over five years, while reported cases in the western town, which installed no plant, held steady. Researchers concluded that the plant caused the decline.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The eastern town's plant removes the two organisms most often responsible for waterborne gastrointestinal illness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Physicians in the eastern town report gastrointestinal illness to the regional registry at the same rate as physicians in the western town, and that rate did not change over the five years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The eastern town's population grew slightly over the five years while the western town's was unchanged.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Residents of both towns drink roughly the same quantity of tap water each day.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The eastern town's council had debated building the filtration plant for a decade before approving it.

questions.explanation: The evidence is *reported* cases, and the conclusion is about illness, so the argument is only as good as the assumption that reporting held steady while illness fell. B secures exactly that, in both towns and across the whole period, which is why it is the strongest. A is the trap: it explains how the plant could work, but a plausible mechanism adds little when a rival explanation for the *numbers* is still open. C cuts the other way — more people should mean more cases, though it does not settle the reporting question. D removes one small difference between the towns without touching the reporting gap, and E is history with no bearing on the inference.

questions.stem:
City planner: Building a light-rail line will reduce traffic congestion downtown, because every comparable city that built one saw congestion fall within five years.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the five years after their light-rail lines opened, the comparable cities adopted no other measures aimed at reducing downtown traffic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Light-rail construction in the comparable cities was completed ahead of schedule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A majority of downtown business owners in the planner's city favor the light-rail proposal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the comparable cities, congestion fell more sharply in outlying neighborhoods than downtown.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proposed line will cost less per mile than any of the comparable cities' lines.

questions.explanation: The argument infers that light rail caused the congestion drop from the fact that the two went together in comparable cities. A strengthens it by ruling out the most natural alternative explanation: if nothing else was done about traffic, the rail line is the likeliest cause. B (schedule), C (popularity) and E (cost) do not bear on whether rail reduces congestion. D, if anything, weakens: the effect showed up where the line was not.
questions.contrast_note: Same argument as the Weaken version. There, the key supplied an alternative cause for the congestion drop (a second policy enacted at the same time). Here the task is reversed, so the key does the reverse job: it rules alternative causes out. Notice that the cost and popularity choices are wrong in both directions, because neither touches the causal link the argument rests on.

questions.stem:
City planner: Building a light-rail line will reduce traffic congestion downtown, because every comparable city that built one saw congestion fall within five years.

The planner's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Light rail is the most cost-effective way for a city to reduce downtown congestion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fall in congestion in the comparable cities was not entirely due to factors unrelated to their light-rail lines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every city that builds a light-rail line sees downtown congestion fall within five years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Downtown congestion in the planner's city has been increasing for at least five years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residents of the comparable cities preferred light rail to expanded bus service.

questions.explanation: The argument moves from 'congestion fell after rail was built' to 'rail will reduce congestion', which needs the drop to have had something to do with the rail. Negate B — the drop was entirely due to unrelated factors — and the argument collapses, so B is required. A and C are stronger than the argument needs (it never claims rail is best, or that the effect is universal). D and E are outside the argument's scope.
questions.contrast_note: Same argument as the Weaken and Strengthen versions, now asked for what it silently relies on. The Weaken key attacked the causal link with a rival cause; the necessary assumption is the modest denial of exactly that attack — rival causes did not do all the work. The two 'too strong' choices here would be fine Strengthen answers, which is the trap: a claim that would help an argument is not thereby one it needs.

questions.stem:
Lawyer: To win the appeal, the defendant must show either that the trial court misapplied the statute or that the jury was improperly instructed. The trial court did not misapply the statute. So if the defendant wins the appeal, then the jury was improperly instructed.

The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A defendant can show that a trial court misapplied a statute only if the court in fact did so.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a trial court misapplies a statute, the defendant will be able to show that it did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The defendant will win the appeal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The jury was improperly instructed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An appeal cannot be won on the ground of improper jury instruction alone.

questions.explanation: The premises say winning requires showing one of two things, and that the court did not misapply the statute. The gap is between the court not misapplying the statute and the defendant being unable to show that it did. A closes it: no misapplication means no showing of one, so the only route left is the jury instruction. B bridges the wrong direction. C and D merely assert parts of the conclusion. E contradicts the premises.
questions.contrast_note: Same argument as the Necessary Assumption version. That task asked for the modest claim the argument cannot do without (that the two listed grounds are the only grounds). This task asks for a claim strong enough to guarantee the conclusion, so the key is a conditional that bridges the actual gap between 'the court did not misapply the statute' and 'the defendant cannot show that it did'. The reversed conditional is the planted trap: it links the same two terms in the direction that proves nothing.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Common-law courts have always preferred bright-line rules to flexible standards.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Modern federal procedure has eliminated all procedural barriers facing pro se litigants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drafters of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure rejected the influence of the common-law tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Twombly and Iqbal returned the federal courts to nineteenth-century pleading standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The shift from rigid pleading to notice pleading reflected a deliberate trade of doctrinal predictability for procedural access.

questions.explanation: The passage's central thesis is that the move to notice pleading was a *trade-off*: the drafters knowingly sacrificed some predictability to widen the courthouse door. E captures both halves. A overstates ('always'). B is contradicted by the closing paragraph. C is too strong — the passage says drafters were *informed by* the tradition, not that they rejected it. D confuses the post-Iqbal tightening with a full reversion.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Twombly and Iqbal is best described as one of…

choices.label: A
choices.text: uncritical endorsement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: open hostility.

choices.label: C
choices.text: qualified concern.

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference.

choices.label: E
choices.text: scholarly bewilderment.

questions.explanation: The author concedes that the cases addressed real problems (mass-tort fishing expeditions) but worries they 'risk reintroducing the very access barrier the 1938 drafters set out to dismantle.' That hedged worry is qualified concern (C), not endorsement, hostility, indifference, or bewilderment.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the original Federal Rules of Civil Procedure took effect in…
questions.explanation: Detail question. The passage states that 'the original Federal Rules of Civil Procedure … took effect in 1938.' 1957 is the year of Conley v. Gibson; the other dates appear nowhere as the adoption year.

questions.stem: The author mentions the Field Code of 1848 primarily in order to…

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that fact pleading was superior to the notice pleading that followed it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate an early reform effort that solved some problems but introduced new ones.

choices.label: C
choices.text: show that New York courts led all other jurisdictions in procedural innovation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that the writ system was never genuinely abandoned.

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that procedural reform inevitably fails.

questions.explanation: The Field Code is introduced as a 'partial remedy' to the writ system, but the next paragraph explains that 'fact pleading … generated its own pathologies.' B captures that role — an early reform that helped yet created new problems. A and E overstate the point; C and D assert claims the passage never makes.

questions.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that defenders of Twombly and Iqbal believe that…

choices.label: A
choices.text: notice pleading should be abolished entirely.

choices.label: B
choices.text: pro se litigants rarely file meritorious claims.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conley v. Gibson was wrongly decided from the outset.

choices.label: D
choices.text: changes in litigation since 1938 justify a more demanding pleading standard.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the Field Code offered a better model than the Federal Rules.

questions.explanation: Defenders 'note that mass-tort and antitrust complaints had created discovery abuses the 1938 drafters could not have foreseen' — i.e., new litigation conditions warrant a tougher standard, which is D. A, B, C, and E go well beyond anything the defenders are said to claim.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Privity of contract was an indefensible doctrine that nineteenth-century courts should have abandoned far sooner than they did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: American products-liability law moved from a privity bar through negligence to strict liability, yet strict liability retains substantial elements of negligence reasoning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: MacPherson v. Buick eliminated the requirement that an injured consumer prove a manufacturer's negligence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Restatement (Second) of Torts settled the long-running dispute over the proper basis of manufacturer liability.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Justice Traynor's concurrence in Escola was the most influential single opinion in the history of American tort law.

questions.explanation: The passage traces an arc — privity bar, then negligence after MacPherson, then strict liability — and closes by stressing that strict liability still 'sits uneasily' with negligence reasoning. B captures both the arc and that tension. A states an evaluative claim the author never makes. C is false: the passage says MacPherson 'did not abolish the need to prove fault.' D is contradicted by the final paragraph, which says the question is still 'debatable.' E overstates a detail and is not the passage's overall point.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the doctrine of privity of contract was crystallized in which one of the following cases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Winterbottom v. Wright.

choices.label: B
choices.text: MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Escola v. Coca-Cola Bottling Co.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Greenman v. Yuba Power Products.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conley v. Gibson.

questions.explanation: Detail question. The first paragraph states that privity of contract was 'crystallized in the English case Winterbottom v. Wright (1842).' MacPherson (B) cracked the privity rule; Escola (C) and Greenman (D) belong to the strict-liability story; Conley v. Gibson (E) is a civil-procedure case that does not appear in this passage at all.

questions.stem: The author refers to Justice Traynor's concurrence in Escola primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that strict liability had already become the governing rule by 1944.

choices.label: B
choices.text: identify an early judicial argument for strict liability that courts would adopt only later.

choices.label: C
choices.text: criticize the Escola majority for reasoning that was internally inconsistent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that Cardozo's approach in MacPherson had been formally overruled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that risk distribution is an inadequate justification for liability.

questions.explanation: The passage presents the 1944 concurrence as urging a change that 'prevailed a generation later' in Greenman (1963) and §402A (1965) — i.e., an early argument adopted only afterward, which is B. A misreads the timeline (it was a concurrence, not the governing rule). C and D describe moves the author never makes. E states a critique the author raises only as one side of a 'debatable' question, not the reason for citing Traynor.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward describing modern products-liability law as 'strict' is best characterized as one of

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic agreement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured skepticism.

choices.label: C
choices.text: outright rejection of strict liability as a concept.

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference to how the doctrine is labeled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: nostalgia for the privity requirement.

questions.explanation: In the final paragraph the author concedes strict liability's risk-distribution rationale but warns that the 'strict-liability label can obscure how much negligence reasoning survives within it' — a hedged, doubting stance toward the label, i.e., measured skepticism (B). A is too positive. C overstates: the author questions the label, not the doctrine's existence. D is wrong because the author plainly cares about the label's accuracy. E finds no support; the author calls privity a remedyless 'price' borne by consumers.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the appellate court in People v. Collins reversed the conviction on which one of the following grounds?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The underlying trait frequencies were unproven, and they were multiplied together as if each trait were independent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The one-in-twelve-million figure was too small to support any inference of guilt.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Statistical evidence is categorically inadmissible in criminal trials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The eyewitnesses' descriptions of the couple conflicted with one another.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The prosecution introduced no physical evidence linking the couple to the crime.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that the court reversed because the individual frequencies 'were never established by evidence' and that multiplying them 'assumed, without proof, that each trait was statistically independent.' A restates exactly that ground. B misreads the objection — the court faulted the figure's foundation, not its size, and the passage never says a small probability cannot support an inference. C overstates: the paragraph on DNA shows statistics are not categorically barred. D and E describe facts (conflicting descriptions, missing physical evidence) the passage never mentions.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the doctrine of prior appropriation differs from the riparian doctrine in that prior appropriation

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats flowing water as a resource held in common by every landowner the stream touches.

choices.label: B
choices.text: forbids any user from depleting the flow so as to defeat a neighbor's reasonable use.

choices.label: C
choices.text: assigns water rights to whoever first diverted the water to a beneficial use, independent of land ownership.

choices.label: D
choices.text: allocates water through time-limited permits issued by an administrative agency.

choices.label: E
choices.text: guarantees every claimant a proportional share of the water during a shortage.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that prior appropriation 'severed water rights from land ownership entirely and awarded them instead to whoever first diverted the water and put it to a recognized beneficial use.' C restates exactly that. A and B describe the riparian doctrine of paragraph 1 (water 'held in common' and the bar on so depleting the flow as 'to defeat a neighbor's reasonable use'), not appropriation. D describes the regulated-riparian permit regime of paragraph 3, not appropriation. E is contradicted: under appropriation a senior holder 'took a full allotment while junior holders received nothing,' so no proportional share is guaranteed.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Court of King's Bench relied on a legal fiction in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: codify a rule that the legislature had declined to enact

choices.label: B
choices.text: conceal from the public the identity of the judges who governed them

choices.label: C
choices.text: hear cases that would otherwise have fallen outside its authority

choices.label: D
choices.text: relieve overcrowding among the prisoners in its custody

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that a fictitious trespass was itself an actionable wrong

questions.explanation: The first paragraph explains that the King's Bench 'could ordinarily try only prisoners already in its custody, so it invented the supposition' of a fictitious trespass — a pretense that 'quietly extended the court's reach far beyond its original bounds.' (C) captures exactly this jurisdiction-expanding purpose and is correct. (A) fails because the passage says 'no statute authorized the maneuver'; the fiction substituted for legislation rather than codifying any rule the legislature had refused to pass. (B) imports Bentham's later charge of deceit, but the paragraph describes the aim as enlarging authority, not hiding the judges' identities. (D) misreads the 'custody,' which was itself the fiction — the court was not thinning out real prisoners. (E) inverts the device: the trespass was a pretense used to reach the case, not a wrong the court sought to establish as actionable.

questions.stem: The author refers to People v. Collins primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: prove that eyewitness identifications are inherently unreliable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate how the appearance of mathematical precision can lend false certainty to an unsupported factual premise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: establish that appellate courts rarely disturb jury verdicts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: endorse the prosecution's method of multiplying trait frequencies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that criminal convictions require a higher probability than civil liability.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Legal fictions are defensible devices whose value depends on their remaining openly recognized as fictions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Legal fictions were indispensable to the early common law but have no place in a modern codified system.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bentham and Fuller reached incompatible conclusions only because they examined different historical periods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fiction of corporate personhood shows why courts should abandon metaphorical reasoning altogether.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Judicial lawmaking is illegitimate whenever it proceeds by way of a fiction rather than open declaration.

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph states the thesis: the author 'leans toward Fuller, but with a qualification' — a fiction 'is worth its cost only so long as it remains visible as a fiction,' since a labeled fiction 'invites the very reform Bentham wanted' while a hardened one 'buries a contestable policy choice.' (A) states exactly this and is correct. (B) echoes Bentham's position, which the author rejects, and the author never says fictions lack a modern place. (C) seizes on the detail that Fuller wrote 'a century later,' but the passage never blames their disagreement on differing eras, and this is not the central claim. (D) misuses the corporate-personhood example, which Fuller offers to show fictions can honestly express, not to condemn metaphor. (E) restates Bentham's rejected view that fiction-based lawmaking is inherently illegitimate.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Bentham would most likely have regarded a legal system's continued reliance on fictions as evidence that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the system's judges were unusually inventive

choices.label: B
choices.text: the system had successfully avoided unjust outcomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: the system relied too heavily on its legislature

choices.label: D
choices.text: the system's litigants preferred flexibility to predictability

choices.label: E
choices.text: the system's written law had not yet been adequately reformed

questions.explanation: Paragraph two reports Bentham's view that a fiction 'was always a confession of failure — proof that the written law had grown inadequate,' and that a codified system 'would dispense with fictions entirely; their persistence was a symptom of arrested legal development.' Combining these, continued reliance on fictions signals to Bentham that the written law remains unreformed, so (E) is correct. (A) contradicts the text, which says persistence was 'not a sign of judicial ingenuity.' (B) overreads: Bentham condemned fictions and would not treat their survival as proof that injustice had been avoided. (C) reverses his commitments — he favored legislative codification and viewed fictions as a sign of too little legislative reform, not excessive reliance on the legislature. (D) attributes the practice to litigants' tastes, a cause the passage never mentions.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Bentham's critique of legal fictions is best described as

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts should abandon their resistance to statistical evidence, which rests on nothing more than innumeracy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People v. Collins demonstrates that probability calculations have no legitimate role in the courtroom.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The law's wariness toward naked statistics is best understood as a demand for individualized, methodologically transparent proof rather than an aversion to numbers.

choices.label: D

questions.stem: The discussion of the gatecrasher hypothetical (the rodeo attendees) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide a real case in which a court awarded damages on statistical evidence alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that the preponderance standard is too lenient for civil cases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: concede that naked statistical evidence is usually sufficient to prove liability.

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that a probability can exceed the applicable burden and still fail for want of individualized evidence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: illustrate the transparent methodology that makes DNA evidence acceptable.
