guides.method: Map the passage's structure, then match the thesis

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: Main-point questions reward structure over detail. Before evaluating choices, reconstruct what each paragraph does — the thesis is usually the through-line, not any single sentence.

steps.title: Map the paragraphs
steps.text: Four paragraphs, one arc: problem → failed fix → deliberate solution → modern contest. The load-bearing move is in paragraph 3: the drafters knowingly traded predictability for access.

paragraphs.gist: Writ-system pleading punished procedural missteps; the Field Code was a partial remedy.
Fact pleading bred its own pathologies; Clark's generation urged mere fair notice.
The 1938 Rules deliberately traded doctrinal predictability for procedural access; Conley cemented it.
Twombly/Iqbal's plausibility threshold — defenders and critics contest whether the bargain is being unwound.

steps.title: State the main point in your own words
steps.text: Something like: the move from rigid pleading to notice pleading was a conscious trade — predictability sacrificed for access — and that bargain is still contested. Now hunt for the choice that captures BOTH halves of the trade.

steps.title: Discard the overreaches
steps.text: A says courts 'always' preferred bright-line rules — extreme and unsupported. B claims all barriers were eliminated — paragraph 4 contradicts it. C says drafters 'rejected' the common-law tradition — too strong; they were informed by it. D equates Twombly/Iqbal with full nineteenth-century restoration — the passage says only 'partial'.

steps.title: The choice with both halves
steps.text: E — the shift reflected a deliberate trade of doctrinal predictability for procedural access — matches the paragraph-3 thesis and the arc of the whole map. E is correct.

guides.method: Read tone from the hedges, not the topic

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: An author-attitude question. Attitude lives in evaluative language — concessions, hedges, worry words — not in the subject matter. Collect the author's actual verbs about Twombly and Iqbal before rating the temperature.

steps.title: Locate the attitude paragraph
steps.text: Your structure map says the modern cases live in the final paragraph — that's where the author's stance shows.

paragraphs.gist: Presents defenders' rationale (unforeseen discovery abuses) AND critics' fear ('risk reintroducing the very access barrier…'), with the author airing both.

steps.title: Weigh the hedges
steps.text: The author grants the cases responded to real problems, yet chooses loaded framing for the downside — 'risk reintroducing the very access barrier the 1938 drafters set out to dismantle.' That is neither cheerleading nor hostility: it's a measured worry with concessions attached. Calibrate the temperature: moderate, negative-leaning, hedged.

steps.title: Match the temperature
steps.text: C — qualified concern — matches a concession-plus-worry stance. A and B are the extremes the hedging rules out, D is contradicted by the author caring enough to flag the risk, and E invents confusion the passage never displays.

guides.method: Locate, verify, and beware neighboring dates

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: 'According to the passage' plus a specific fact = a detail question. Do not answer from memory — locate the line, because detail questions bait you with other numbers that appear nearby in the text.

steps.title: Know where facts live
steps.text: Your paragraph map says dates and rule history live in paragraph 3 (adoption era) and paragraph 4 (modern cases). Go to paragraph 3 for the Rules' effective date.

paragraphs.gist: Fact pleading's pathologies; Clark's notice-pleading idea.
Original Federal Rules take effect; Rule 8(a)(2); Conley v. Gibson (1957).

steps.title: Disarm the decoys
steps.text: 1848 belongs to the Field Code (paragraph 1) — and 1948 echoes it. 1957 is Conley v. Gibson, the case that later cemented the standard. 1966 and 1975 appear nowhere in the passage. Every decoy is a real number from the wrong sentence.

steps.title: Read the line itself
steps.text: Paragraph 3 states the original Federal Rules 'took effect in 1938.' A is correct.

guides.method: Ask what work the detail does for the author

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: 'Primarily in order to' asks for the detail's FUNCTION, not its content. The answer describes what the mention accomplishes in the author's structure — so the structure map, not the sentence alone, decides it.

steps.title: Place the detail in the arc
steps.text: The Field Code appears at the hinge between paragraph 1 (problem) and paragraph 2 (the fix's own failure). It is introduced as a 'partial remedy' — and the very next paragraph opens with fact pleading generating 'its own pathologies'.

paragraphs.gist: Writ system punishes missteps; Field Code of 1848 offered a partial remedy (fact pleading).
Fact pleading generated its own pathologies — setting up the notice-pleading idea.

steps.title: Phrase the function yourself
steps.text: The Field Code's job in the passage: show an early reform that fixed part of the problem but created new ones — a stepping stone that motivates the next reform. Look for a choice saying exactly that, at that temperature.

steps.title: Discard the wrong temperatures
steps.text: A reverses the author's stance (nothing says fact pleading beat notice pleading). C inflates one example into a leadership claim. D contradicts the passage — the writ system WAS replaced. E turns one bumpy reform into 'reform inevitably fails', far beyond the author's measured tone.

steps.title: The matching function
steps.text: B — illustrate an early reform effort that solved some problems but introduced new ones — is precisely the stepping-stone role the map shows. B is correct.

guides.method: Attribute the view to the right speaker

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: An inference question about what DEFENDERS of the cases believe — not the author, not the critics. Misattribution is the trap: find the one sentence the passage puts in the defenders' mouths and stay inside it.

steps.title: Locate the defenders' sentence
steps.text: Paragraph 4 assigns each camp exactly one position — keep them separate on your map.

paragraphs.gist: Defenders: mass-tort and antitrust complaints created discovery abuses the 1938 drafters could not have foreseen. Critics: the new standard risks restoring the old access barrier.

steps.title: Paraphrase the defenders' logic
steps.text: Their point: litigation changed after 1938 in ways that produced abuse, so the old permissive standard no longer fits — newer conditions justify a tougher threshold. The right answer will restate that modest claim; wrong answers will overshoot it (abolish notice pleading, condemn Conley) or smuggle in claims about litigants the defenders never made.

steps.title: Match the inference
steps.text: D — changes in litigation since 1938 justify a more demanding pleading standard — is the direct paraphrase. A and C overshoot into abolition and retroactive error, B smears pro se litigants without textual basis, and E resurrects the Field Code, which nobody in paragraph 4 endorses.

writing_rubrics.name: Argumentative Writing — analytic rubric
writing_rubrics.summary: Five weighted criteria read across four bands. LSAC does not publish a numeric score for the writing section — admissions readers read the sample itself — so this rubric is a study instrument for diagnosing a draft, not a predictor of any official result.

bands.label: Developing
bands.descriptor: The reader can identify an attempt but has to supply the connective work themselves.

bands.label: Adequate
bands.descriptor: The moves are present but thin — asserted rather than argued, or handled unevenly across the response.

bands.label: Strong
bands.descriptor: The moves are present, deliberate, and carry their weight; a reader is persuaded even where they disagree.

bands.label: Exemplary
bands.descriptor: The response anticipates the reader's resistance and disarms it before it forms.

criteria.name: Position and thesis
criteria.description: Takes one defensible position on the stated issue and holds it. Readers should be able to state the writer's claim in a sentence after the first paragraph.
look_for: A thesis that names the position and the principal reason for it
A position that is actually contestable rather than a truism
The same position at the end as at the beginning

band_notes.1: The reader cannot tell which side the writer is on, or the position drifts mid-response.
band_notes.2: A position is stated but reads as a restatement of the prompt rather than a claim of the writer's own.
band_notes.3: A clear, contestable thesis with its principal reason attached, held throughout.
band_notes.4: A thesis precise enough to rule things out — the reader knows what evidence would refute it.

criteria.name: Reasoning and evidence
criteria.description: Supports the position with reasons that actually bear on it, and makes the connection between reason and claim explicit rather than leaving it to the reader.
look_for: Each supporting paragraph states a reason, not just a topic
The warrant linking reason to thesis is stated, not assumed
Claims are calibrated — hedged where the support is partial

band_notes.1: Assertions accumulate without support, or support is offered for a claim the thesis never made.
band_notes.2: Reasons are present but the link to the thesis is left implicit; the reader does the joining.
band_notes.3: Each reason is stated, supported, and explicitly tied back to the thesis.
band_notes.4: Reasoning is calibrated to its support — strong where the ground is firm, qualified where it is not.

criteria.name: Engagement with the given perspectives
criteria.description: Uses the perspectives supplied with the prompt as material to reason from, rather than restating them or ignoring them.
look_for: At least two of the supplied perspectives are engaged substantively
A perspective is interpreted or weighed, not merely quoted
A perspective that cuts against the position is not silently dropped

band_notes.1: The perspectives are ignored, or listed back without use.
band_notes.2: One perspective is used; the rest are decorative or absent.
band_notes.3: Several perspectives are weighed and put to work for the argument.
band_notes.4: A perspective that appears to cut against the position is reinterpreted so that it supports it, or is honestly conceded.

criteria.name: Counterargument and concession
criteria.description: States the strongest version of the opposing position and answers it, conceding what genuinely must be conceded.
look_for: The opposing position is stated in a form its holders would accept
The response answers the objection rather than repeating the thesis
Concessions are real and are bounded so they do not swallow the claim

band_notes.1: No opposing position appears, or it appears only as a caricature.
band_notes.2: An objection is named but answered by restating the thesis more loudly.
band_notes.3: The strongest objection is stated fairly and given a real answer.
band_notes.4: A genuine concession is made and then bounded, leaving the thesis standing on narrower but firmer ground.

criteria.name: Organization and written expression
criteria.description: Orders the argument so each paragraph earns its place, and writes clearly enough that the reasoning is never obscured by the prose.
look_for: A reader can predict what each paragraph will do from its first sentence
Transitions carry argumentative weight, not just sequence
Sentence-level clarity; errors do not impede meaning

band_notes.1: Order appears arbitrary, or errors force the reader to reread to recover the meaning.
band_notes.2: A recognizable structure with paragraphs that overlap or wander; occasional interference from errors.
band_notes.3: Purposeful structure and clean prose; the argument is easy to follow.
band_notes.4: Structure that is itself an argument — each paragraph placed where it does the most work.

writing_prompts.title: Transit expansion or arterial widening
writing_prompts.issue: Should the city council spend its one-time infrastructure grant on extending the light-rail line, or on widening the arterial road that carries commuter traffic into downtown?
writing_prompts.context: Fairhaven has received a one-time state infrastructure grant that will fund exactly one of two shovel-ready projects. The council has committed to deciding on the record and has published four staff perspectives. The grant cannot be split, deferred, or matched with local funds.

positions.name: Extend the light-rail line
positions.summary: Run the existing line four stops further into the northern neighbourhoods, adding three stations.

positions.name: Widen the arterial
positions.summary: Add one lane in each direction to Culver Avenue, the principal commuter route into downtown.

perspectives.text: Traffic engineering staff project that widening Culver Avenue would cut average peak commute times by nine minutes in its first year, and by four minutes by year six as new drivers fill the added capacity.

The three northern neighbourhoods the rail extension would serve have the city's lowest rates of household car ownership; residents there currently reach downtown by a bus route that runs every forty minutes.
The rail extension costs roughly twice as much per projected daily rider as the road project costs per projected daily driver.
A council member notes that the arterial widening can be completed in eighteen months, while the rail extension would take four years and disrupt two commercial blocks throughout.

writing_prompts.task: Write an argumentative essay taking a position on the issue above. Argue for one of the two positions and against the other. Use at least two of the supplied perspectives as material for your reasoning, state the strongest case against your position, and answer it. There is no correct position — only a well-argued one.

model_response.thesis: The council should fund the rail extension, because it is the only one of the two projects that changes what is possible for residents who cannot drive.
model_response.essay:
The council should fund the rail extension. Both projects would move people downtown faster, but only one of them reaches people who currently cannot get there at all — and when a grant can be spent once, that difference should decide it.

The case rests on a standard, not merely on a fact. The fact is perspective 2: the three northern neighbourhoods have the city's lowest car-ownership rates and are served today by a forty-minute bus. The standard is that a one-time transport investment should be judged first by whether it reaches people who have no alternative, and only second by how much time it saves people who already have one. A driver on Culver Avenue whose commute is nine minutes shorter has a better version of a trip they were already making. A resident in the northern neighbourhoods gains a trip they were effectively priced out of. Those are not the same kind of gain, and treating them as interchangeable minutes is what the per-rider comparison quietly does.

The engineering projection in perspective 1 makes the point sharper rather than weaker. The nine-minute saving decays to four minutes by year six as new drivers fill the lane. That is the ordinary behaviour of added road capacity: it is absorbed. A grant spent on the arterial buys six years of shrinking benefit; a grant spent on rail buys a station that is still there in thirty.

The strongest case for the road is perspective 3, and it should be stated at full strength: the rail extension costs about twice as much per projected daily rider. If cost-effectiveness is the test, the road wins outright. But cost per rider ranks options by who already travels a given way — it takes today's ridership as the denominator when the entire purpose of the extension is to change that denominator. A metric that penalizes a project for serving a population that does not yet travel cannot be the metric for deciding whether to serve them.

One concession is real. Perspective 4 is right that four years of construction, and disruption to two commercial blocks throughout, is a genuine cost borne by identifiable people. The council should mitigate it and should say so on the record. But eighteen months against four years is an argument about sequencing a durable asset, not an argument against acquiring one — and it does not reach the standard the choice actually turns on.

The road project is the better answer to the question of how to make an existing commute faster. The council is answering a different question: who gets to make the commute at all.

annotations.note: The thesis names the position and its principal reason in one sentence ('the only one of the two projects that changes what is possible for residents who cannot drive'), and the close restates it without softening.
Paragraph two states the warrant explicitly — 'the case rests on a standard, not merely on a fact' — instead of letting the car-ownership statistic stand as though it argued for itself.

Three of the four perspectives are put to work, and the two that cut against the position (3 on cost, 4 on disruption) are engaged rather than skipped. Perspective 1 is reinterpreted so that its own decay figure supports the thesis.

The cost-per-rider objection is stated at its strongest ('If cost-effectiveness is the test, the road wins outright') and then answered by denying its warrant — the metric measures the wrong denominator — not by restating the thesis.
Each paragraph's first sentence announces its job: thesis, standard, reinterpretation of the engineering projection, the strongest objection, the bounded concession, close.

self_check.prompt: Can a reader state your position and your principal reason for it after reading only your first paragraph?
For each reason you gave, did you say why it bears on your claim — or did you leave the reader to supply the link?
Did you put at least two supplied perspectives to work, and did you handle the one that cuts against you rather than dropping it?
Would someone holding the opposing position recognize their own view in how you stated it, and did you answer it rather than restate your thesis?
Can a reader predict what each paragraph will do from its opening sentence?

writing_prompts.title: Mandatory pro bono hours before licensure
writing_prompts.issue: Should the state bar require every applicant for admission to complete fifty hours of supervised pro bono legal work before being licensed?
writing_prompts.context: The state bar's admissions committee is considering a rule requiring fifty hours of supervised pro bono work as a condition of licensure. The committee has published four perspectives from its consultation. Any rule adopted would apply to all applicants beginning with the next admissions cycle.

positions.name: Adopt the requirement
positions.summary: Make fifty hours of supervised pro bono work a condition of admission for every applicant.

positions.name: Decline to adopt it
positions.summary: Leave pro bono service voluntary and encouraged, as it is today.

perspectives.text: Legal-aid organizations in the state report turning away roughly two of every three eligible applicants for lack of capacity.
Supervising a novice costs a legal-aid organization staff time; two directors estimate that a fifty-hour placement consumes between eight and fifteen hours of an experienced attorney's time.

Applicants who work during law school, or who have dependants, have materially less unpaid time available than applicants who do not; a jurisdiction that adopted a similar rule saw admission delayed by a term for a disproportionate share of such applicants.
A committee member argues that a professional obligation the profession will not require of its entrants is one it does not really hold.

writing_prompts.task: Write an argumentative essay taking a position on the issue above. Argue for one of the two positions and against the other. Use at least two of the supplied perspectives as material for your reasoning, state the strongest case against your position, and answer it. There is no correct position — only a well-argued one.

model_response.thesis: The bar should decline to adopt the requirement, because a rule that conscripts unpaid labour from the applicants least able to give it is a poor instrument for a shortage caused by underfunding.
model_response.essay:
The bar should decline to adopt the fifty-hour requirement. The unmet need it responds to is real and the motive behind it is honourable, but the rule aims a licensing condition at a funding problem, and it charges the cost of doing so to the applicants least able to pay it.

Start with what the requirement would actually produce. Perspective 1 establishes the shortage: legal-aid organizations turn away two of every three eligible applicants. Perspective 2 establishes what a mandated placement costs the organization receiving it — eight to fifteen hours of an experienced attorney's time for every fifty hours of novice work. That ratio matters because it means the rule does not simply add capacity; it converts scarce supervisory capacity into abundant unsupervised capacity. Whether that trade helps depends on whether the work an unlicensed novice can competently do is the work that is going undone. Nothing in the consultation suggests it is, and the committee has not asked.

The distributional objection is heavier still. Perspective 3 reports that in a jurisdiction with a comparable rule, admission was delayed by a term for a disproportionate share of applicants who worked during law school or had dependants. A licensing condition denominated in unpaid hours is not a uniform burden; it is a burden that scales inversely with an applicant's resources. The profession would be selecting, at the threshold, for applicants who can afford to work for free — and it would be doing so in the name of serving people who cannot afford lawyers. That is a standard defeating itself.

The strongest case for the rule is perspective 4, and it deserves to be stated without hedging: a professional obligation the profession will not require of its entrants is one it does not really hold. That is a serious claim about the integrity of an aspiration, and it is largely right. But it argues for requiring the obligation of the profession, not of its applicants. The bar's members are licensed, insured, competent, and paid; its applicants are none of those things. If the obligation is real, the rule that expresses it is a requirement on practitioners — who can discharge it competently and can afford to — not a toll collected at the door from people with the least capacity to pay it.

One concession is owed. Declining this rule leaves perspective 1's shortage exactly where it is, and 'fund legal aid properly' is the answer of a body that does not control the appropriation. The bar should therefore not merely decline; it should say what it will do instead, and a mandatory hours rule for admitted members is the obvious candidate.

A profession that will not fund access to justice does not acquire it by requiring free labour from the people waiting to be let in.

annotations.note: The thesis states the position and its reason together, and the reason is specific enough to be refutable — a reader knows that showing the burden falls evenly would damage it.

The supervision-ratio paragraph does not stop at the statistic; it states what the ratio implies (scarce supervisory capacity converted into abundant unsupervised capacity) and names the unexamined assumption the committee has not tested.
All four perspectives are used, and the one that most supports the opposing position (4) is given the essay's longest treatment rather than being minimized.

The rebuttal grants that perspective 4 is 'largely right' and then answers by redirecting its scope — the obligation binds practitioners, not applicants — which defeats the objection without denying its premise.
The concession paragraph is placed last-but-one so the reader leaves with the bounded answer, and it names a concrete alternative rather than conceding into vagueness.

self_check.prompt: Can a reader state your position and your principal reason for it after reading only your first paragraph?
For each reason you gave, did you say why it bears on your claim — or did you leave the reader to supply the link?
Did you put at least two supplied perspectives to work, and did you handle the one that cuts against you rather than dropping it?
Would someone holding the opposing position recognize their own view in how you stated it, and did you answer it rather than restate your thesis?
Can a reader predict what each paragraph will do from its opening sentence?

writing_prompts.title: Narrative evaluations in place of letter grades
writing_prompts.issue: Should the law school replace letter grades with written narrative evaluations in all first-year courses?
writing_prompts.context: A law school's curriculum committee is deciding whether to replace first-year letter grades with written narrative evaluations. Four perspectives were submitted during faculty and student consultation. The decision applies to the first year only; upper-year courses would continue to be graded.

positions.name: Replace letter grades with narrative evaluations
positions.summary: First-year courses produce a written evaluation of each student's work and no letter grade.

positions.name: Keep letter grades
positions.summary: First-year courses continue to be graded on the existing curve.

perspectives.text: A survey of the school's first-year students found that the majority described grade anxiety as the single largest impediment to their learning; faculty report that students rarely take intellectual risks in graded first-year work.

Judicial clerkship hiring and many employer screens filter on first-year grade point average, and several hiring partners have said an unranked transcript would move an applicant to a slower review track.
Writing a substantive narrative evaluation takes an experienced instructor between twenty and forty minutes per student; first-year sections at the school average ninety students.
Two schools that made this change report that informal proxies for rank — faculty recommendations, journal membership, and section reputation — became more important in hiring rather than less.

writing_prompts.task: Write an argumentative essay taking a position on the issue above. Argue for one of the two positions and against the other. Use at least two of the supplied perspectives as material for your reasoning, state the strongest case against your position, and answer it. There is no correct position — only a well-argued one.

model_response.thesis: The school should keep first-year letter grades, because removing a visible ranking does not remove ranking — it moves it somewhere students cannot see, contest, or earn.
model_response.essay:
The school should keep letter grades in the first year. The harm the proposal identifies is real, but the mechanism it proposes does not remove that harm; it relocates it into channels that are less fair than the one it replaces.

The argument turns on what a grade is for. A grade does two jobs: it tells a student how their work was read, and it tells outsiders how that work compared. The proposal assumes these can be separated — that the first job can be done better in prose while the second simply lapses. Perspective 4 is the evidence that it does not lapse. At two schools that made this change, the comparative judgement did not disappear; it migrated to faculty recommendations, journal membership, and section reputation. Every one of those is less transparent than a grade, less contestable by a student who thinks it wrong, and more responsive to who an instructor happened to notice. Anxiety about an unseen ranking is not obviously smaller than anxiety about a seen one, and it is certainly harder to act on.

Perspective 2 makes the cost concrete rather than speculative. Clerkship and employer screens filter on first-year GPA, and hiring partners have said an unranked transcript slows review. A school may decide its students should bear that cost for a pedagogical gain. But it should not tell itself that the cost is borne evenly: the student with family in the profession is the one for whom the informal channels of perspective 4 already work.

The strongest case for the change is perspective 1, and it should be stated at full force: a majority of first-year students name grade anxiety as the single largest impediment to their learning, and faculty observe that graded first-year work makes students risk-averse. If that is right, the current system is failing at teaching, which is the school's actual job. The answer is that the finding indicts the *stakes* attached to first-year grades, not the existence of a grade. A compressed curve, a pass threshold for the first semester, a policy that first-year grades are not reported to employers before a fixed date — each addresses the anxiety while keeping a ranking that a student can see and appeal. The proposal treats the most drastic available instrument as the only one.

Perspective 3 is a genuine cost of the proposal but should not be overstated: twenty to forty minutes per student across ninety-student sections is a real institutional burden, though a school that judged the change right could fund it. It is a reason for care, not a reason for refusal, and the argument does not need it.

Keep the grade; fight the stakes. A ranking students can see is the one they can argue with.

annotations.note: The thesis is contestable and specific — it claims relocation rather than elimination, which tells the reader exactly what evidence would refute it (a school where informal proxies did not intensify).
The second paragraph supplies the warrant by defining what a grade is for, so perspective 4's finding has a standard to bear on instead of standing as a bare fact.
All four are engaged, and perspective 3 is explicitly *de-weighted* as a reason for care rather than refusal — a calibration move that strengthens the argument by refusing support it does not need.

The rebuttal concedes that perspective 1 may show the current system is failing at teaching, then answers by scope: the finding indicts the stakes, not the grade, and three narrower instruments are named.
Paragraph openings are all directional, and the close compresses the argument into a contrast rather than restating it.

self_check.prompt: Can a reader state your position and your principal reason for it after reading only your first paragraph?
For each reason you gave, did you say why it bears on your claim — or did you leave the reader to supply the link?
Did you put at least two supplied perspectives to work, and did you handle the one that cuts against you rather than dropping it?
Would someone holding the opposing position recognize their own view in how you stated it, and did you answer it rather than restate your thesis?
Can a reader predict what each paragraph will do from its opening sentence?

writing_prompts.title: Cameras in the appellate courtroom
writing_prompts.issue: Should the national court of appeal permit live video broadcast of its oral arguments?
writing_prompts.context: A national appellate court is reconsidering its rule barring cameras from oral argument. Live audio is already released; written transcripts appear the same day. Four perspectives were submitted to the court's rules committee. The court's decisions bind every lower court in the jurisdiction.

positions.name: Permit live video broadcast
positions.summary: Argument is streamed live in video, as audio already is.

positions.name: Retain the bar on cameras
positions.summary: Live audio and same-day transcripts continue; video remains barred.

perspectives.text: Since live audio was introduced, listenership has grown steadily and no member of the court has reported a change in how counsel or the bench behave during argument.

A judge argues that video invites the excerpting of a single exchange — a judge's sharp question, an advocate's stumble — circulated without the surrounding argument, and that this reshapes what advocates and judges say more than an audio feed does.
Legal journalists report that audio-only coverage systematically under-reports argument, because outlets that lead with video have no visual material and run the story shorter or not at all.

Two comparable courts that adopted video report no measurable change in the length or tone of argument after five years, though both note that the number of arguments excerpted in political advertising rose.

writing_prompts.task: Write an argumentative essay taking a position on the issue above. Argue for one of the two positions and against the other. Use at least two of the supplied perspectives as material for your reasoning, state the strongest case against your position, and answer it. There is no correct position — only a well-argued one.

model_response.thesis: The court should permit video, because the harm it fears is a harm of decontextualized excerpting that the audio feed already permits, while the benefit — that the public sees the reasoning that binds them — is available in no other way.
model_response.essay:
The court should permit live video of oral argument. The objection to it is serious and specific, but it identifies a harm the court has already accepted, and it weighs that harm against a benefit it has not credited.

The court's own experience is the strongest available evidence. Perspective 1 reports that live audio has grown its audience for years with no member of the court observing any change in how counsel or the bench behave. Perspective 4 reports the same absence at two comparable courts five years after adopting video. Two independent bodies of evidence, one internal and one external, point the same way: the behavioural effect that justifies the bar has not appeared where it was predicted. A rule maintained against a predicted harm should be reconsidered when the prediction has been tested twice and failed.

Perspective 3 supplies the benefit, and it is the perspective the objection never engages. Outlets that lead with video run argument coverage shorter, or not at all, when only audio exists. The consequence is not that the public receives a worse account of the court's reasoning; it is that it receives no account and forms its impression from the decision alone. A court whose judgments bind every lower court in the jurisdiction has an interest in the public seeing that its decisions are reasoned rather than merely announced. That interest is not served by a transcript almost no one reads.

The strongest objection is perspective 2, and it should be put at full strength: video invites the excerpting of a single exchange — a sharp question, a stumble — circulated without the argument around it, and the prospect of that shapes what an advocate is willing to say. This is a real mechanism, and perspective 4's finding that political excerpting rose is evidence that it operates.

But it does not distinguish video from what the court already does. Audio is excerptible; a fifteen-second clip of a judge's question travels perfectly well without pictures, and the same-day transcript is quotable in print. The court accepted decontextualized excerpting when it released audio. What video changes is the volume of the excerpting, not its nature — and perspective 4 is the direct test of whether that volume changes behaviour. It reports that it did not, at two courts, over five years. The objection predicts an effect; the evidence assembled for this decision looks for that effect and does not find it.

The concession is that this evidence is about two courts and about tone and length — the things that can be measured. It cannot rule out a subtler chilling: an advocate who does not press an unpopular argument, a judge who does not test a position they intend to adopt. That possibility warrants monitoring, and a court adopting video should say what it would count as evidence of it and commit to revisiting the rule. It does not warrant continuing to bar the one form of coverage that reaches the people the court's judgments bind.

annotations.note: The thesis carries both halves of the argument — the harm is already accepted, the benefit is uniquely available — so the reader knows in advance which two claims the essay must make good.

The evidence paragraph is careful about what two null findings license: it claims a failed prediction, not a proven absence, and the concession paragraph later names exactly what the measurements could not detect.

All four are used, and perspective 4 is used against itself — the same study that reports rising political excerpting also reports no behavioural change, and the essay makes that tension the pivot of the rebuttal.

The objection is stated at full strength and conceded to be a real mechanism with supporting evidence; it is then answered by showing it does not distinguish video from the audio the court already releases — a parity argument, not a denial.

The rebuttal is deliberately split across two paragraphs — statement, then answer — so the objection is allowed to land before it is met, and the close converts the concession into a monitoring commitment rather than a hedge.

self_check.prompt: Can a reader state your position and your principal reason for it after reading only your first paragraph?
For each reason you gave, did you say why it bears on your claim — or did you leave the reader to supply the link?
Did you put at least two supplied perspectives to work, and did you handle the one that cuts against you rather than dropping it?
Would someone holding the opposing position recognize their own view in how you stated it, and did you answer it rather than restate your thesis?
Can a reader predict what each paragraph will do from its opening sentence?

library.title: Answer-Choice Elimination
library.summary: Why elimination beats selection, the language patterns that mark wrong answers, and the discipline of reading every choice to its end.

spans.text: The exam is built so that four choices are wrong for identifiable reasons and one is right for a reason that is often subtle. Hunting for the right answer means evaluating five candidates against a vague standard. Eliminating means applying four specific tests, each of which is easier.

Concretely: read all five choices before committing. Test takers who select the first choice that sounds good miss a specific, common item — the one where choice B is attractive and choice D is correct.

items.text: Cross out anything that fails on shape.
Wrong question type answered, wrong direction, wrong kind of sentence. This is fast and removes one or two.
Cross out anything requiring outside information.
If you have to supply a fact, it is not supported.
Cross out anything about the wrong object.
Weakens a subsidiary claim, describes the wrong paragraph, addresses a different conclusion.
Compare the survivors on a single dimension.
Usually scope or strength. Name the dimension explicitly rather than re-reading both hoping one feels better.

spans.text: Step 4 is where accuracy is won. "I'll read them both again" is not a method. "B says
all
, D says
some
, and the stimulus only supports
some
" is.

items.text: . Usually too strong on inference and RC questions.
A concept appearing in the choice and nowhere in the stimulus. Almost always a distractor.
The right terms in the wrong direction, especially with conditionals. See
Accurate about the passage, unresponsive to the stem. The single most common wrong-answer type in Reading Comprehension.
Correct through the first clause and defective after. The defect is usually at the end.

spans.text: That last one is why the rule is:
read every choice to its final word.
The exam knows people commit early.
Stem: which one of the following most accurately states the main point?
Choice: "The traditional account of the treatise's reception is inaccurate because it relies on sales figures, which recent archival evidence has shown to be fabricated."
The first two thirds are right — the traditional account is challenged, and it did rest on sales figures. The final clause is the defect: the passage said the sales figures were
accurate but incomplete as a measure of influence
, not fabricated.
A reader who commits after "relies on sales figures" picks this. A reader who finishes the sentence eliminates it in a second.
When two choices survive, the difference is almost always one of:

items.text: — one covers more than the text supports, or less than the question asked.
— one asserts more confidently than the evidence licenses.
— they are about different things: the argument versus a premise, the author versus a cited theorist.
— one has the causal or conditional relationship reversed.

spans.text: Name which of the four is in play. If you cannot name it, you are probably comparing on feel, and feel is what the distractor was built for.

blocks.title: Falling in love with a choice

spans.text: You read choice B, it matches your pre-phrase, and you stop reading. The exam builds this trap constantly: B is close to the pre-phrase and D is the pre-phrase.
The pre-phrase is a filter, not an answer. It tells you what to look for. Check all five against it, then choose the best match — not the first acceptable one.

blocks.text: After the exam, review your eliminations

spans.text: In review, do not just check the right answer. For every wrong choice, state the reason it fails, in the vocabulary above. The reasons repeat, and after fifty questions you will recognise the distractor patterns on sight. That is the core of
Blind Review

items.text: Eliminate against four specific tests rather than hunting for the right answer.
Read all five choices, every time, to the final word — defects hide at the end.
Watch for extremes, new terms, reversals, true-but-irrelevant, and half-right choices.
When two survive, name the dimension — scope, strength, object, or direction.
In review, articulate why each wrong choice is wrong. The patterns repeat.

outline.text: After the exam, review your eliminations

library.title: Argument Anatomy — Finding the Conclusion
library.summary: Every Logical Reasoning question rests on separating what is being claimed from what is offered in support of it. This is how to do that reliably in under twenty seconds.

spans.text: Almost every Logical Reasoning stimulus is built from three kinds of sentence, and telling them apart is the prerequisite for every other technique in this library.

items.text: — the claim the author wants you to accept. There is exactly one main conclusion.
— a claim offered as a reason to accept something else.
— context that orients you but supports nothing. Frequently the first sentence.

spans.text: A fourth appears in harder stimuli: the
subsidiary conclusion
, a claim that is supported by a premise
and
supports the main conclusion. It is the single most common wrong answer on main-conclusion questions, because it genuinely is a conclusion — just not the one being asked for. See
Main Conclusion
Indicator words help —
therefore
thus
so
hence
consequently
point forward to a conclusion;
because
since
for
given that
after all
point backward to a premise — but they are absent or misleading often enough that they cannot be your primary tool.
The reliable method is a question. Take the sentence you suspect is the conclusion and ask:
why does the author think this?
If the rest of the stimulus answers, you have the conclusion. Then reverse it: take a candidate premise and ask
what does this get me?
If the answer is another sentence in the stimulus, you are holding a premise.

Municipal composting programmes reduce landfill volume. The city's new programme diverted 4,000 tonnes last year. Critics note the programme costs more per tonne than landfilling. But cost per tonne is the wrong measure, because landfill capacity is finite and replacing it is far more expensive than any composting subsidy. The programme should be expanded.

Test "The programme should be expanded." Why does the author think so? Because cost per tonne is the wrong measure, because capacity is finite. The rest of the stimulus answers — so it is the conclusion.
Test "Cost per tonne is the wrong measure." Why? Because capacity is finite. That also has support — so it is a
subsidiary
conclusion, supported by one thing and supporting another. On a main-conclusion question this is the trap answer, and it will look extremely attractive.

items.text: which the author's own view begins. Everything before is frequently someone else's position being set up for rejection.
introduce a position the author is usually about to attack. Mistaking an attributed view for the author's conclusion is a top-three beginner error.
— recommendations and judgements are conclusions far more often than they are premises.

spans.text: Beginners reach for the final sentence. On easy items that works often enough to feel like a rule, which is precisely what makes it dangerous: the exam writes hard items where the conclusion sits first or in the middle, and the last sentence is a restated premise or an implication the author is
not
claiming. Run the why-test even when the last sentence looks obvious.
Once you can locate the conclusion, the rest of Logical Reasoning becomes tractable:

items.text: is an unstated claim the argument needs to get from premises to
is to attack the support for
conclusion, not to contradict a premise — see
is a defect in the move from premises to
question asks what one sentence does relative to

spans.text: Every one of those definitions has "that conclusion" in it. Get the conclusion wrong and the correct answer becomes unfindable no matter how good your technique is.

items.text: Three sentence roles: conclusion, premise, background — plus subsidiary conclusions in harder items.
Indicator words help but are not reliable; the why-test is.
Attributed views and the sentence before a pivot are usually not the author's conclusion.
Subsidiary conclusions are the classic main-point trap: supported
Every other LR technique is defined relative to the conclusion, so this step is not optional.

library.title: Blind Review
library.summary: The single highest-return study habit — re-solving without the clock and without the key before you check anything, and what the gap between the two scores tells you.

spans.text: Ordinary review — check the key, read the explanation for the ones you missed — teaches very little. Reading an explanation produces recognition ("yes, that makes sense") which feels like learning and is not. You have not practised the retrieval; you have watched someone else do it.
Worse, ordinary review cannot distinguish the two reasons you missed a question, and they need completely different fixes:

items.text: to do it. A method problem.
and did not have time, or rushed. A pacing problem.

spans.text: Blind review separates them cleanly, which is why it is worth the time it costs.

items.text: Mark every question you are not fully certain about — a dot in the margin is enough. Do not skip this; the marking is what makes the method work.
Re-solve every marked question with unlimited time
, no clock, no key. Take as long as you want. Write down, for each one, what you now think the answer is and
, and why each other choice fails.
Your timed score and your blind-review score.
, and only for questions you got wrong in blind review.

spans.text: The distance between the two scores is the diagnosis.

rows.text: You have the method; the clock is the problem
Method problem; more time does not help
Drill that family untimed until accuracy rises
Method is solid; you are rushing decisions
Slow the early questions, bank time deliberately

spans.text: A large gap is
good news
— it means the points are already within reach and the fix is procedural. A small gap means the reasoning is not there yet, and no amount of pacing work will produce it.

blocks.title: Two students, same score, opposite prescriptions

spans.text: Both score 17 of 25 on the same section.
Student A

blind-reviews to 24. Given time, they can do nearly everything. Their loss is entirely clock-driven — they spent four minutes on two hard questions and rushed the last six. Prescription: triage practice and checkpoint discipline. Drilling more assumption questions would waste a month.
Student B

blind-reviews to 18. Given unlimited time they still cannot do these questions. Their loss is method. Prescription: untimed drilling by family, starting with whichever family the error log flags. Pacing practice would only produce faster wrong answers.
Identical scores. Opposite study plans. Nothing except blind review distinguishes them.

blocks.text: The "why each wrong answer is wrong" rule

spans.text: During blind review, for every question, write a sentence on each of the four wrong choices. This is the part people skip and it is where most of the value sits.
The reasons repeat — extreme language, new term, reversed relationship, true but irrelevant, half-right — and articulating them fifty times is what turns
Answer-Choice Elimination
from something you have read into something you do automatically.

blocks.title: What to write for a question you got right

spans.text: If you were certain and correct, write nothing and move on.
If you were
uncertain

and correct — a marked question — treat it exactly like a miss. A lucky right answer is a miss that has not happened yet, and the marking system exists precisely to catch these. Students who only review actual errors leave their most unstable questions untouched.
Reading a good explanation is pleasant, feels productive, and teaches close to nothing, because the hard part — generating the reasoning yourself — has been done for you.
The explanation is a
check

on your blind-review reasoning, not a substitute for it. Read it after you have committed to an answer and written down why. If you find yourself reading explanations first, you have reverted to ordinary review.

Blind review roughly doubles the time a section costs: 35 minutes to take it, 30 to 45 to review it. That ratio is correct. A study plan that is 90% new questions and 10% review buys repetition of existing errors; see
Building a Study Plan That Survives Contact

items.text: Mark uncertainty during the timed section; the marking makes everything else work.
Re-solve marked questions untimed before looking at any key or explanation.
Score twice. The gap diagnoses method problems versus pacing problems.
Write why each wrong choice fails — the reasons repeat, and articulating them builds the reflex.
Review time should roughly equal drilling time. Explanations come last, as a check.

outline.text: The "why each wrong answer is wrong" rule

library.title: Building a Study Plan That Survives Contact
library.summary: A phased plan — diagnose, build method, drill by type, then simulate — with honest volume estimates and the failure modes that waste the most months.

blocks.text: Start with a diagnostic, not with lessons

spans.text: Take one full timed practice exam before you study anything. Not to get a good score — to get a
shape

. The diagnostic answers three questions no curriculum can answer for you: which section costs you the most raw points, whether your losses come from running out of time or from being wrong unhurried, and which question families you miss disproportionately.

Those three answers determine everything downstream. A test taker who misses fifteen Logical Reasoning questions because they never reach the last eight has a pacing problem and should not spend March learning conditional notation. A test taker who misses fifteen with time to spare has a method problem, and pacing drills will do nothing for them.

blocks.title: Two identical scores, two opposite plans

spans.text: Both score 152. The first left nine questions blank across two LR sections and got 90% of what they attempted right. The second answered everything and got 70% right.

The first needs triage and pacing: they already have the method and are being robbed by the clock. The second needs method: going faster would only produce wrong answers sooner. Handing both the same "eight-week LR course" wastes one of them entirely.

items.text: Argument structure, conditional logic, causal reasoning. Untimed. The goal is that you can name what an argument is doing before you look at the choices. Start with
Phase 2 — Method by question type (4 to 8 weeks).
One family at a time: read the family guide, drill twenty to thirty items of only that family, review every one. This is where most of the score comes from, and where most plans skip ahead too early.
Phase 3 — Mixed drilling and pacing (3 to 6 weeks).
Full sections under time. The skill being built is not the reasoning — it is the triage and the clock discipline in
Full four-section exams, same time of day as your real administration, same breaks, no pausing. Sit at least four.

spans.text: Phases overlap at the edges. They do not reorder: simulating before you have method just produces a stable record of the same mistakes.

Roughly 250 to 300 hours is the common figure for a substantial improvement, spread over three to six months. Compressing that into six weeks does not work well, because the binding constraint is not hours — it is the number of
review cycles
your reasoning gets to run through. You need to be wrong, see why, and meet the same pattern again a week later.
A workable weekly shape for someone with a job:

rows.text: 45–60 min drilling one question family, plus full review
30 min review of the error log, no new questions
A full timed section or, in phase 4, a full exam
Blind review of that section or exam

spans.text: Note the ratio. Review time is roughly equal to drilling time. Anyone whose plan is 90% new questions and 10% review is buying repetition of their own errors.
Score-chasing.
Taking practice exams weekly to watch the number. Exams are a measurement instrument and a poor teaching one; you have a finite supply and they teach least per hour.
Drilling without reviewing.
Two hundred questions skimmed teaches less than forty reviewed properly. See
Blind Review
Studying your strengths.
Logical Reasoning feels good when you are good at it. The error log exists to override that instinct; see
The Error Log
Re-plan on trends, not on a single result. A practice score four points below your average is inside normal variance, as
Scoring, Scaling, and What a Point Is Worth
explains. Change the plan when three consecutive data points point the same way, or when the error log shows a family you have drilled twice and still miss at the same rate — that one means the
method
is wrong, not the volume.

items.text: Diagnose first. The same score can mean a pacing problem or a method problem, and they need opposite plans.
Four phases in order: foundations, method by type, mixed pacing, full simulation.
Budget roughly 250–300 hours over three to six months; review time should roughly equal drilling time.
Practice exams measure, they do not teach. Spend them sparingly and late.
Re-plan on trends of three, never on a single test.

outline.text: Start with a diagnostic, not with lessons

library.title: Causal Reasoning — Correlation, Cause, and the Four Attacks
library.summary: How the exam builds causal arguments from correlational evidence, and the four standard ways every causal claim can be attacked or defended.

blocks.text: The shape of a causal argument

spans.text: An enormous share of Logical Reasoning stimuli follow one template: the author observes that two things go together, and concludes that one causes the other.

lines: Premise:     X and Y are correlated (or X preceded Y)
Conclusion:  X causes Y

spans.text: Recognising this template is worth more than any individual technique, because the moment you see it you already know the four ways it can be attacked and what the credited answer will look like. See
Causation vs. Correlation
Every weaken answer to a causal argument is one of these, and every strengthen answer is one of them denied.

items.text: Some third factor Z causes Y instead. This is the most common credited weakener on the exam. See
Y causes X, not the other way round. Especially available when the stimulus only establishes that the two occur together, never which came first.
The correlation is chance, or the sample was too small or too odd to establish anything. See
Cause without effect, or effect without cause.
A case where X happened and Y did not, or Y happened with no X. A single well-chosen counterexample undercuts a general causal claim.

spans.text: To
strengthen
the same argument, deny one of the four: rule out the alternative cause, establish the temporal order, add a controlled comparison, or show the effect tracks the cause across cases.
Employees at firms with open-plan offices report 30% more sick days than employees at firms with private offices. Open-plan layouts must therefore be damaging employee health.
Alternative cause:
open-plan firms are concentrated in industries with younger workforces and more generous sick-leave policies, so days are
reported
more freely.
Reverse causation:
firms with high absenteeism restructure into open plans to improve supervision.
Coincidence or sampling:
the comparison covers eleven firms in one city over one winter.
Effect without cause:
private-office firms in the same industry show the same 30% gap year over year.
Each of these is a plausible credited answer to "which most weakens". Generating them
before
reading the choices is the technique; see
Strengthen and Weaken

blocks.text: Signals that a causal claim is being made

spans.text: The conclusion does not have to contain the word "cause". Watch for:

items.text: A recommendation that depends on causation:
to reduce Y, do less X

spans.text: That last one is easy to miss. "The city should ban open-plan offices" is a causal argument wearing a policy hat, and the four attacks apply unchanged.

A choice that denies the correlation itself — "employees at open-plan firms actually report fewer sick days" — feels devastating and is usually wrong. The exam expects you to accept the premises as given and attack the
inference
. A choice that contradicts a stated premise is more often a trap than a credited answer, because the argument's defect is the leap from correlation to cause, not the correlation.
Causal stimuli lean heavily on statistics, and two moves recur often enough to name:

items.text: of something is not a rise in the
, and vice versa, unless the base population held steady. See
A study establishes something about the group studied. Whether it generalises depends on how that group was selected, which the stimulus frequently declines to tell you.
Correlation-to-cause is the exam's most common argument template. Learn to see it instantly.
Four attacks: alternative cause, reverse causation, coincidence or bad sample, and cause-without-effect.
Strengthening is denying one of the four, most often ruling out an alternative cause.
Causal claims hide inside recommendations and inside verbs like "leads to" and "explains".
Attack the inference, not the premise; a choice that denies the data is usually a trap.

outline.text: The shape of a causal argument

library.title: Conditional Logic — Necessary, Sufficient, and the Contrapositive
library.summary: Translating if/then language into notation, taking contrapositives reliably, chaining conditionals, and recognising the two invalid moves the exam tests constantly.

references.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Classical Logic

spans.text: A conditional says: whenever the first thing holds, the second must hold too. Write it
S → N

items.text: for N — S happening is enough to guarantee N.
for S — without N, S cannot happen.

spans.text: The two are not interchangeable and the exam's entire conditional apparatus rests on that. "All lawyers passed the bar" gives you
Lawyer → Passed bar
. It does
not
give you that everyone who passed the bar is a lawyer. See
Conditional Reasoning
The hard part is never the logic. It is turning English into the right arrow.

rows.text: Negate the "unless" term, it becomes sufficient

spans.text: Two of these cause most errors.
"Only if" attaches to the necessary condition
— "you may vote only if you are a member" is
Vote → Member
, not the reverse. And
"unless"
is best handled mechanically: negate the term attached to "unless" and make it the sufficient condition. "The filing is late unless it arrives Friday" becomes
NOT Arrives Friday → Late
For any
A → B
, the contrapositive
NOT B → NOT A
is logically equivalent — same statement, said from the other end. Take it by
flipping the terms and negating both

lines: Original:        Enforceable → Both parties signed
Contrapositive:  NOT Both parties signed → NOT Enforceable

spans.text: The contrapositive is where roughly half of all conditional inferences on the exam actually live, because the exam writes stimuli that trigger the negative end. Taking it should be automatic; see
Contrapositive
Every application reviewed in the first round was complete. Only complete applications included a financial statement. Ramirez's application did not include a financial statement.
Translate:

lines: First round      → Complete
Complete         → Financial statement

spans.text: Chain them:
First round → Complete → Financial statement
, so
First round → Financial statement
Contrapositive of the chain:
NOT Financial statement → NOT First round
Ramirez has no financial statement. Therefore Ramirez's application was not reviewed in the first round. That is the credited inference, and note that it was only reachable from the contrapositive.
The exam tests these relentlessly, both as wrong answers and as the flaw in flaw questions.

items.text: . Wrong: B can arrive by other routes.
All lawyers passed the bar. Kim passed the bar. Therefore Kim is a lawyer.
Kim might be a paralegal who sat it.
All lawyers passed the bar. Kim is not a lawyer. Therefore Kim did not pass.

spans.text: The two
valid
moves are modus ponens (
A → B
A
, therefore
B
— see
Modus Ponens
) and modus tollens (
A → B
NOT B
, therefore
NOT A
— see
Modus Tollens
). Everything else with one conditional and one fact is invalid.

Notation is a tool for stimuli that are genuinely conditional and genuinely tangled. Diagramming a causal argument or a two-sentence stimulus with one conditional in it costs more time than it saves, and a chain of five arrows you built under time pressure is a new source of error. Diagram when there are two or more conditionals to combine, or when "unless" and "only if" appear together. Otherwise, translate in your head and move.

items.text: : the sufficient condition guarantees, the necessary condition is required. They are not symmetric.
"Only if" and "requires" mark the necessary term; "unless" means negate-and-make-sufficient.
The contrapositive flips and negates, and is where a large share of credited inferences live.
Chain conditionals through shared terms, then take the contrapositive of the whole chain.
Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are the two invalid moves, and the exam tests both constantly.

library.title: The Error Log
library.summary: What to record about every miss so that a month of drilling produces a diagnosis instead of a feeling, and the four error causes that need four different fixes.

spans.text: Without a record, your sense of your own weaknesses is built from the questions that annoyed you most, which is not the same as the questions that cost you most. People consistently report struggling with the families they find unpleasant rather than the ones they miss.

A log converts that into a count. After two weeks it will tell you something you did not know, and it is frequently unwelcome — the family you thought was fine turns out to be a quarter of your losses.
One row per miss. Six fields, which fit on a phone note or a spreadsheet.

rows.text: B; it sounded like something the author assumed
Negating D destroys the argument; negating B does not
On necessary assumption, negate before comparing

spans.text: The last two fields are the ones that matter. A log of question numbers and topics is a list; a log of
rules carried forward
is a study plan.
Every miss has one of four causes, and they need four different responses. Assigning the cause is the single most valuable thing the log does.

items.text: You did not know how to attack this family.
read the family article, drill twenty of that family untimed.
You knew the method and misapplied it — negated sloppily, misread the stem, mapped the wrong paragraph.
a specific checklist rule, applied deliberately for a week.
You would have got it with another minute.
pacing and triage, not content. See
You misread the stimulus, the stem, or the choice.
slow the read, not the reasoning. Frequently this is the largest category and the most fixable.

spans.text: Blind review is what makes the assignment possible, because it separates clock from method directly. See
Blind Review

blocks.title: What two weeks of logging reveals

spans.text: A test taker believes their weakness is parallel reasoning, which they find exhausting. Two weeks of logging, 38 misses:

lines: Necessary assumption    9   (7 method, 2 execution)
Flaw                    7   (5 reading — misread the stem, 2 method)
Parallel                4   (3 clock, 1 method)
RC inference            8   (6 reading, 2 method)
Strengthen/weaken       5   (4 execution — attacked a premise)
Other                   5

spans.text: Parallel reasoning is fourth, and three of its four misses are clock — meaning triage would fix them without any content work. The real story is that 13 of 38 misses are
reading
errors, split between misread flaw stems and RC inference.
The prescription that falls out: a week on necessary assumption method, and a deliberate habit of re-reading the stem before the choices. Neither was what this person would have guessed.
Weekly, ten minutes. Three questions:

items.text: Which family has the most misses?
Method means content work; reading means a slow-down rule; clock means pacing; execution means a checklist.
Are last week's carried-forward rules working?
If the same rule appears three weeks running, it is not being applied — make it a pre-question ritual instead of an intention.

spans.text: That third question is where logs usually fail. A rule written and never applied is a record of a good intention, and the fix is to attach it to a moment: "before reading choices on any assumption question, negate."
A log with thirty fields per row stops being maintained inside a week. Six fields, thirty seconds per entry, and only for misses and uncertain-but-correct answers.
The log you actually keep beats the comprehensive one you abandon.

items.text: Memory over-weights the families you dislike; a log counts what actually costs you.
Six fields per miss, and the two that matter are why the credited answer wins and the rule to carry forward.
Assign one of four causes: method, execution, clock, reading. Each needs a different fix.
Review weekly for ten minutes; drill the family with the most misses.
A rule appearing three weeks running is not being applied — attach it to a moment.

library.title: The Flaw Catalog
library.summary: The recurring reasoning defects the exam names, what each looks like in a stimulus, and the abstract phrasing the credited answer will use.

spans.text: Flaw questions, parallel-flaw questions, and a large share of weaken and assumption questions all reward the same skill: naming the defect in your own words before you read the choices. Naming is easier when you have a vocabulary, and the exam reuses a small set of defects far more often than a list of "logical fallacies" would suggest. See
Flaw in the Reasoning

The credited answer will describe the defect in abstract terms — "takes for granted that", "confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one", "draws a general conclusion from an unrepresentative sample". Matching your own plain-language name to that abstraction is the whole task.

items.text: Treats something required as something that guarantees, or vice versa. Answer phrasing:
"treats a condition that is necessary as if it were sufficient."
The single most common named flaw on the exam.
Affirming the consequent / denying the antecedent.
The two invalid conditional moves from
"infers that because a condition is met, its cause must have occurred."
"infers a causal relationship from a mere correlation."
"fails to consider that another factor may account for the observed effect."
Treats sequence as causation because one thing followed another.
Generalises from a group chosen in a way that does not represent the whole. See
Treats the absence of evidence for a claim as evidence that it is false, or absence of disproof as proof. See
Slides between a rate and a count. See
Appeal to inappropriate authority or popularity.
Rests a factual claim on who said it or how many believe it.
One word carries two meanings across the argument, and the argument only works if you do not notice. Answer phrasing:
"relies on a term that is used in different senses."
The conclusion appears among the premises, restated. Answer phrasing:
"presupposes what it sets out to establish."
Attacks a position the opponent did not take.
Attacks the source rather than the claim.
Infers from properties of parts to the whole, or the reverse.
Presents two options as exhaustive when others exist.
Conflating what is with what ought to be.
Moves from a description to a prescription without a bridging principle.

spans.text: The commission's report cannot be trusted. Two of its seven authors previously consulted for the utility companies whose rates the report evaluates.

Name it first: the argument rejects a claim by pointing at who made it, without engaging the report's content — and it generalises from two authors to the whole document. That is an ad hominem with a part-to-whole move stacked on it.
Now the credited answer is findable:
"rejects a position on the basis of the affiliations of some of those who advanced it, without addressing the reasoning offered in support of it."
Had you gone straight to the choices, three of them would have sounded reasonable.
The most dangerous distractor on a flaw question describes something the argument genuinely does — but not its defect.
"Relies on the testimony of experts"
may be perfectly accurate and completely beside the point. The test is not "is this true of the argument" but "is this why the argument fails". Run every surviving choice against that question;
Flaw Questions
has the full method.

items.text: The exam reuses a small catalog of defects. Learn the names and the abstract phrasings.
Necessary–sufficient confusion and correlation-to-cause are the two most frequent.
Name the flaw in plain language before reading the choices; then match to the abstraction.
Half-right distractors are accurate descriptions of irrelevant features — the standard trap.

library.title: Triage and Guessing
library.summary: No penalty for wrong answers means every bubble gets filled — plus how to decide which questions to abandon, when, and what to guess.

spans.text: There is no penalty for a wrong answer. A blank and a wrong answer score identically, so a blank is a guess you declined to make — strictly worse. See
Scoring, Scaling, and What a Point Is Worth
Two practical rules follow:

items.text: Reserve the last 30 seconds of every section
to fill any remaining bubbles. Set it as a checkpoint, not an intention.
Pick one letter and use it for all blind guesses.
Answer keys are close to evenly distributed, so a consistent letter is as good as any other choice — and it removes a decision at the moment you least want one.

blocks.text: Triage is a skill, not an admission

spans.text: Deciding which questions to abandon is a scored skill. The exam contains, in every section, a small number of questions that will cost you three minutes and that you will probably still miss. Trading those for three questions you would get right is straightforwardly correct, and the only reason people resist it is that skipping feels like losing.
Skip candidates, roughly in order:

items.text: Six arguments to analyse. Highest time cost on the section. See
late in a section when you are behind.
Any question where after 45 seconds you cannot state what the answer needs to do.
That is the strongest signal available, and it is available early.

spans.text: They are different decisions and confusing them is expensive.
The pre-emptive skip.
You look at the question and decide before starting. Costs about five seconds. This is the good one, and it is available only if you glance at what is coming.
The abandonment.
You have invested ninety seconds and stop. Costs the ninety seconds. Necessary sometimes, but it is a loss being cut, not a decision being made well.

Building the pre-emptive skip is what pacing practice is for. A test taker who can identify a three-minute question in five seconds has a structural advantage over one who discovers it two minutes in.
A section leaves you four minutes for the last four questions. One is a parallel-flaw question.
No triage:
you take them in order. The parallel question eats 150 seconds and you miss it anyway. Ninety seconds remain for three questions; you rush and get one right.
Score: 1 of 4.
With triage:
you glance ahead, guess the parallel question immediately, and spend 80 seconds each on the other three, getting all three right. The guess has a 20% chance.
Expected score: 3.2 of 4.
The gap is more than two raw points, from one decision that took five seconds.

blocks.text: Guessing well when you have looked

spans.text: A blind guess is 20%. An educated guess after even minimal work is much better, and the work is cheap:

items.text: A choice introducing a term that appears nowhere in the stimulus is rarely credited.
On weaken and strengthen, eliminate anything that denies a premise.

spans.text: Fifteen seconds of that raises a 20% guess to 33% or 50%. Across five guessed questions that is one to one and a half raw points.

You guess, intend to return, and do not mark the question. At the end of the section you have four minutes and no idea which questions to revisit, so you spend them re-reading questions you already answered correctly.
Flag every guess, always, even when you are sure you will remember. Especially then.

items.text: No wrong-answer penalty: every bubble gets filled, with a pre-chosen letter for blind guesses.
Reserve the last 30 seconds of each section for sweeping up blanks.
Triage is a scored skill; the pre-emptive skip costs five seconds, the abandonment costs ninety.
If you cannot say what the answer must do after 45 seconds, that is your signal.
Fifteen seconds of elimination turns a 20% guess into a 33–50% one. Always flag guesses.
