library.title: Game Types and Question Types
library.summary: Sequencing, grouping, selection, distribution and hybrid games, plus the question types each one asks and the shortcut that answers the first one every time.

items.text: Entities in order. Rules are relative (
Entities distributed among named categories, with capacity rules. See
A single yes-or-no: which entities are chosen. Rules are almost entirely conditional, and the contrapositive does most of the work. See
The counts themselves are the puzzle — how many go in each group, before you decide who. See
Two dimensions at once, usually order plus a category. Build a grid; do not try to hold the second dimension mentally. See

spans.text: Acceptability.
Which one of the following could be a complete and accurate list?

Always the first question, and never solved by reasoning. Take each rule in turn and scan the five choices for a violation. One rule usually kills one choice, and four rules clear the board in under forty seconds. See
Rule-Elimination
Must be true / could be true.
Answered from the master diagram plus your up-front inferences. If your inferences were thorough these are lookups; if not, they are five separate mini-games.
Could be true EXCEPT / must be false.
Read the stem twice. Four choices are possible and one is impossible, and losing track of the polarity is the commonest error in the section. See
Could Be True EXCEPT
Local conditional.
If R is fourth, which one of the following must be true?
Redraw a
fresh
copy of the board with the new condition, work its consequences, answer, then discard it. Never write a local condition onto the master diagram.
Maximum / minimum.
What is the greatest number of…
Usually a numeric-distribution question in disguise; work the counts before the placements. See
Maximum / Minimum
Rule substitution.
Which one of the following, if substituted for the third rule, would have the same effect?
The hardest question type in the section. The credited answer must produce exactly the same set of possible boards — no more, no fewer. See
Rule Substitution
Rules: Q before T. If P is second, S is fifth. R and V consecutive. P not first.

lines: (A) P Q R V S T   → P is first. Violates rule 4. Out.
(B) Q P R V T S   → P second, S is sixth not fifth. Violates 2. Out.
(C) Q R V P T S   → check all: Q before T yes; P not second so rule 2
is inert; RV consecutive yes; P not first yes. Survives.
(D) T Q R V P S   → T before Q. Violates rule 1. Out.
(E) Q R P V T S   → R and V not consecutive. Violates 3. Out.

spans.text: Answer (C), reached in about thirty seconds with no diagram work at all. Rule-by-rule scanning across the choices is faster than choice-by-choice checking against the rules, because one rule can eliminate several choices in a single pass.

items.text: — it is free, and the surviving choice is a valid board you can reuse as a hypothetical later.
— each one is self-contained and produces a concrete board, and those boards answer global questions afterwards.
— by then you have three or four real boards on the page, and a single counterexample kills a "must be true" choice instantly.

spans.text: That ordering is not stylistic. Doing globals first means reasoning abstractly; doing them last means checking against boards you already built.

A local question says "if R is fourth". Two questions later you are still treating R as fourth. This is the most common way to lose a whole game, and it is entirely preventable: draw local conditions on a separate line, and cross them out the moment the question is answered.

items.text: Five game types; identify which one before notating, because it decides the board.
Acceptability questions are pure elimination — scan by rule, not by choice.
Local conditionals get a fresh board that is discarded immediately after.
Answer in order: acceptability, locals, then globals against the boards you built.
EXCEPT and must-be-false stems invert the task; misreading polarity is the top error.

library.title: Inferences and Frames
library.summary: The up-front work that turns a fifteen-minute game into a six-minute one — how to combine rules, when to split the game into frames, and how to know you are done.

spans.text: After the board is drawn, spend two minutes deriving what the game did not say. Inferences come from a short list of sources, and running the list is more reliable than waiting for insight.

items.text: Two rules mentioning the same entity almost always combine.
, which fixes Q out of the last two slots and V out of the first two.
A two-slot block plus a barred slot eliminates several placements at once.
Count entities against capacity. A game with seven entities and groups of at most three, three, and two has no slack anywhere.
Every conditional's negative end. Games are written to trigger them.
Whichever element appears in the most rules is where the game is decided. Start there.

spans.text: Five lectures — F G H J K — are given on five consecutive days. G is before H. J is before G. K is not on day one or day five.
Chain:
J … G … H
. Three entities in a fixed relative order.
Now count. J needs at least two entities after it, so J is on day one, two, or three. H needs at least two before it, so H is on day three, four, or five. K is barred from days one and five.
Combine: if J is not on day one, the only remaining candidates for day one are F or G — and G cannot be first because J precedes it. So
day one is J or F
, always. That single inference answers a large share of the question set and took about forty seconds.

When a game has a rule that forces a small number of possibilities, draw them all out. Two or three complete boards beat one abstract diagram, because every subsequent question becomes a lookup rather than a derivation.
Frame when you see:

items.text: A rule with exactly two options —
either P or Q is selected, not both
A block with only two or three viable positions.
A numeric split with limited options —

spans.text: Do not frame when the branching runs to five or more boards. Past three or four, drawing them costs more than the questions save.

lines: Rule: H is first or last.
then RV block fits              then RV block fits

spans.text: Each frame then absorbs the remaining rules, and most questions resolve to "true in both frames" (must be true), "true in one" (could be true), or "true in neither" (cannot be true).

Two minutes on inference, then move. The signal to stop is that a full pass through the sources above produces nothing new. Test takers who keep hunting for one more inference lose more time than the inference would have saved.
Conversely, the signal that you stopped too early is finding yourself doing the same derivation inside two different questions. If you deduce something twice, it belonged on the master diagram.

A local question produces a valid, complete board. Most people answer the question and erase it. That board is evidence: it is a concrete counterexample that can instantly kill a "must be true" choice on a later question.
Keep every complete board you build, numbered, off to the side. By the fourth question you usually have three of them, and global questions become a scan across boards rather than fresh reasoning.

items.text: Work the inference sources as a checklist: shared entities, blocks against restrictions, numbers, contrapositives, most-restricted element.
Frame when a rule forces two or three possibilities; do not frame past four.
Two minutes of up-front inference, then stop — but if you derive something twice, it belonged on the master board.
Keep every complete hypothetical you build; they answer later global questions for free.
The most-constrained entity or slot is where every game is decided. Start there.

library.title: Logic Games — Section Guide
library.summary: Analytical Reasoning left the scored exam in August 2024, and remains the best available trainer for the constraint tracking that conditional Logical Reasoning rewards.

spans.text: LSAC removed Analytical Reasoning from the scored LSAT in August 2024. A modern administration has no Logic Games section, and no study plan should treat it as a scoring priority. See
How the LSAT Is Built
It stays in this library and in the drill bank for one concrete reason: it is the cleanest available practice at
holding several formal constraints at once and drawing consequences from them

. That is precisely the skill that conditional Logical Reasoning questions test under time pressure, and games train it in a purer, more diagnosable form than LR does — when you get a game wrong you can see exactly which inference you failed to make.
Treat it as a gym, not as an exam section. Twenty minutes on a grouping game is a legitimate way to spend a study session in phase 1 or 2 of
Building a Study Plan That Survives Contact
; it is not a legitimate substitute for LR drilling in phase 3.
A game gives you an
inventory
of entities, a
structure
to place them into, and a set of
rules
constraining the placement. Then it asks four to seven questions, most of which are about what must, could, or cannot be true.

lines: Setup:  Seven applicants — F G H J K L M — are interviewed
one at a time, in order, on seven consecutive days.
Rules:  G is interviewed before J.
H is interviewed either first or last.
K and L are interviewed on consecutive days.

spans.text: The work splits three ways, and the proportions matter: roughly 40% of your time on the setup and notation, 30% on up-front inferences, 30% on the questions. People who rush the setup pay for it on every question; people who never move past the setup run out of clock.

items.text: Turning rules into marks you can see at a glance. See
Combining rules to derive what the game did not tell you — the step that separates a fifteen-minute game from a six-minute one. See
Knowing which question types can be answered from the master diagram and which require a hypothetical. See

spans.text: Take the setup above and add:
M is interviewed on day four.

Work the combination before answering anything. H is first or last. K and L are a consecutive block, and day four is taken by M — so the KL block fits in days one-two, two-three, five-six, or six-seven. If H takes day one, KL cannot use days one-two, and so on.
Two minutes spent here collapses most of the question set into lookups. Skipping it means rebuilding this reasoning inside every single question, five times over, under the clock.

blocks.text: What transfers to the scored exam

items.text: Games force correct handling of "unless", "only if", and contrapositives, because a mis-translated rule produces a board that visibly fails. See
The habit of asking "what are all the possibilities" is directly the habit that answers must-be-true and cannot-be-true questions in LR.
concrete, and that distinction decides a whole LR family. See

spans.text: If Logic Games is enjoyable and you have time, use it in phase 1 and 2 as conditional-logic training. If it is not, skip it entirely — nothing on the scored exam requires it, and the same reasoning is trainable through conditional LR drilling. The one thing not to do is spend phase 3 on it, which is where scored-section pacing has to be built.

items.text: Analytical Reasoning left the scored exam in August 2024; it is a trainer, not a section.
Setup and up-front inference deserve roughly 70% of the time spent on a game.
Games train constraint tracking, conditional translation, and must-versus-could in a diagnosable form.
Use it early in a study plan, if at all; never at the expense of phase-3 LR pacing work.
Skipping it entirely is a defensible plan. Substituting it for LR drilling is not.

library.title: Game Setup and Notation
library.summary: Choosing the right board for the game, a compact and unambiguous notation for every common rule, and the setup errors that cost whole games.

blocks.text: Pick the board from the structure

spans.text: Before writing a single rule, decide what the game is asking you to build. Three boards cover the large majority.

items.text: — when entities are ordered or assigned to numbered positions. Draw the positions as a row of underscores.
— when entities are distributed among categories. Draw one column per group, with capacity marked if the game gives it.
— when two attributes are assigned to each entity, or when entities are matched across two dimensions.

spans.text: Getting this wrong is the most expensive setup error, because every rule then has to be recorded in a shape that does not hold it well. If a game distributes six interns among three departments across two shifts, that is a grid, and drawing it as three columns loses the shift dimension.
Compactness matters: notation you have to decode is notation that slows you down.

rows.text: K and L consecutive, order unknown
Exactly one of P or Q
At least one of T, U

spans.text: Two habits are worth building.
Always write the contrapositive
underneath a conditional rule — the game will trigger the negative end, and deriving it under pressure is where errors come from. And
put negative rules on the board
, not in the margin: a "not M" written under slot three is seen; one written in a list is looked up.

Six files — P Q R S T V — are shelved on six numbered shelves, one per shelf. Q is shelved somewhere before T. If P is on shelf two, then S is on shelf five. R and V are on consecutive shelves. P is not on shelf one.

lines: Inventory: P Q R S T V   (6 entities, 6 slots, one each)
^ NOT P
Rules:  Q … T
P2 → S5        (contrapositive: NOT S5 → NOT P2)
[RV]

spans.text: Everything is now visible in one glance: the slot restriction sits on the board where it applies, the conditional carries its contrapositive, and the block is bracketed. No rule needs to be re-read from the prompt again.

items.text: A reversed conditional produces a board that is wrong in a way you will not notice until three questions have gone against you. Translate deliberately; see

Not every game places exactly one entity per slot. Check whether entities repeat, whether slots can be empty, and whether the counts match — a game with seven entities and five slots behaves completely differently.
Capacity constraints are rules and belong on the board, written above the group they govern.
Rewriting the rules instead of notating them.
Copying rules out in sentences produces a second prompt to read, not a diagram.

spans.text: Before starting the questions, count. How many entities, how many slots, can slots be empty, can entities repeat? A surprising share of hard games are hard entirely because of a numeric constraint stated in one clause of the setup — "at least two but no more than four" — that most readers absorb as flavour text.
The numbers frequently produce the game's most powerful inference before you have combined a single pair of rules. See
Inferences and Frames

items.text: Choose the board first: linear slots, group columns, or a grid.
Notate compactly; write every conditional's contrapositive beneath it.
Put negative and capacity constraints on the board, not in a margin list.
Check whether the game is one-to-one before assuming it.
Count entities against slots before answering anything — the numbers often carry the key inference.

library.title: The Assumption Family
library.summary: Necessary versus sufficient assumptions, the negation test that settles necessary questions, and why the two subtypes need opposite instincts.

spans.text: Both subtypes ask about something unstated that the argument relies on, and their stems differ by a few words.

items.text: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
The credited answer is something the argument
— without it the argument collapses. It is usually modest, sometimes almost trivially so.
Which one of the following, if assumed, allows the conclusion to be properly drawn?
The credited answer is something that, added to the premises,
the conclusion. It is usually strong, often stronger than seems necessary.

spans.text: The instincts are opposite. On necessary questions a choice that seems too weak is often right and a strong one is usually wrong. On sufficient questions a choice that seems too weak is wrong, because it leaves the gap open. See
Necessary Assumption
and
Sufficient Assumption
Both subtypes are solved the same way up to the last step: locate the
gap
— the term or idea that appears in the conclusion but not in the premises, or vice versa.

lines: Premises talk about:   hours of training completed
Conclusion talks about: competence on the job
Gap:                    training hours ↔ competence

spans.text: Almost every credited answer in this family bridges exactly that gap. Pre-phrasing it before reading the choices turns a five-way judgement call into a matching exercise.
For necessary assumptions only, there is a mechanical check that settles nearly every hard item.
Negate the choice. If the argument falls apart, the choice is necessary. If the argument survives, it is not.

Negate precisely — the negation of "all" is "not all", the negation of "will" is "will not necessarily". Over-negating produces a statement so strong that it damages any argument, which makes every choice look correct.
The city's new bike lanes have not reduced congestion: traffic speeds on the affected corridors are unchanged since the lanes opened. So the lanes should be removed.
Gap: from "have not reduced congestion" to "should be removed" — the argument needs congestion reduction to be the standard by which the lanes are judged.
Candidate:
"The bike lanes provide no benefit that would justify keeping them apart from congestion reduction."
Negated:
"The bike lanes do provide some other benefit that would justify keeping them."
The argument now fails — removal no longer follows.
Necessary.
Candidate:
"Traffic speed is the only accurate measure of congestion."
Negated:
"Traffic speed is not the only accurate measure."
The argument is weakened but not destroyed; speed can still be evidence.
Not necessary
— this is a strengthener wearing an assumption costume.

blocks.text: Sufficient assumptions and the conditional bridge

spans.text: Sufficient-assumption stimuli are frequently conditional. Translate the premises and the conclusion into arrows, and the credited answer is almost always the arrow that completes the chain.

lines: Premise:     Applied → Interviewed
Conclusion:  Applied → Hired
Missing:     Interviewed → Hired

spans.text: If the chain has a hole, the answer plugs it exactly. Do not accept a choice that plugs it partially or that runs the wrong direction —
Hired → Interviewed
looks similar and does nothing.

The most attractive wrong answer in this family is a statement the author would probably endorse, about a topic the argument mentions, that the argument does not actually need. Agreement is not the test. On necessary questions the test is negation; on sufficient questions the test is whether the conclusion now
follows
. Neither test is "does this feel like something they assumed".

Take any assumption item and ask both questions of the credited answer: is it required, and is it enough? A necessary assumption is usually not sufficient, and a sufficient one is often not necessary. Items like
reward noticing which one the stem asked for.

items.text: Necessary assumptions are required; sufficient assumptions are enough. Opposite instincts on strength.
Find the gap between premise terms and conclusion terms before reading any choice.
Negate the choice to test necessity; if the argument survives, it was not necessary.
Negate precisely — over-negation makes every choice look required.
On conditional sufficient-assumption items, the answer is the missing arrow, in the right direction.

outline.text: Sufficient assumptions and the conditional bridge

library.title: Completing the Argument
library.summary: The fill-in-the-blank family — how the connector word before the blank tells you what kind of sentence belongs there, and why the answer is almost always a conclusion.

spans.text: The stimulus ends mid-sentence and the stem reads
which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

This looks like its own family but it is really a delivery mechanism: the blank can sit where a conclusion goes, where a premise goes, or where an explanation goes, and the sentence leading into it tells you which. See
Completing the Argument
Roughly three quarters of the time the blank takes a
conclusion
, which makes this family a close relative of the inference questions in
Inference Questions
— with the important difference that the credited answer only has to be well supported, not airtight.
The words immediately before the blank are the instruction. Read them first and read them carefully.

rows.text: A conclusion drawn from what precedes
A premise that supports what precedes
A condition, in the right logical direction
Something that cuts against what precedes
An explanation of the preceding claim

spans.text: Getting this wrong is the family's characteristic error: supplying a perfectly good conclusion when the connector called for a premise produces a sentence that is true, on-topic, and grammatically impossible in the slot.

Municipal libraries that extended their evening hours saw circulation rise by 15%, while those that kept standard hours saw no change. The increase cannot be attributed to a general rise in reading, because ______
The connector is
because
, so the blank is a
premise supporting
the claim that the rise is not a general trend.
Correct shape:
"libraries that kept standard hours drew from the same neighbourhoods and saw no increase at all."
That is evidence for the claim.
Wrong shape, and highly attractive:
"the extended hours caused the increase in circulation."
That is a fine conclusion and a terrible premise — it restates what the author is trying to establish rather than supporting it, which makes the argument circular. See
Circular Reasoning

items.text: , then decide what kind of sentence the blank takes.
Read the stimulus for the gap.
What is the argument missing to get where it is going?
— a choice of the wrong kind is wrong even if it is true.

spans.text: Step 4 is where the time is saved. On a
because
blank, every choice that reads like a conclusion can go without evaluating its content at all.

Because the stimulus is incomplete, several choices will be consistent with it and add nothing. They restate a premise, or they assert something plausible about the topic that the argument does not need.

The check: read the completed argument aloud with the choice in the blank. If the argument does not get stronger or does not now reach its conclusion, the choice is inert — and inert is wrong, however true.

blocks.text: When the blank takes a conclusion

spans.text: Treat it as a most-strongly-supported question. The standard is not certainty; it is that the choice is better supported by the stimulus than the other four. Prefer modest wording, prefer the choice you can trace to specific text, and be suspicious of anything introducing a new term that appeared nowhere above the blank.

items.text: The connector immediately before the blank tells you what kind of sentence belongs there.
Most blanks take a conclusion; a substantial minority take a premise or an explanation.
Eliminate on sentence type before evaluating content — it removes several choices instantly.
A premise that restates the conclusion makes the argument circular; that is a trap, not an answer.
On conclusion blanks, apply most-strongly-supported standards: modest, traceable, no new terms.

outline.text: When the blank takes a conclusion

library.title: Flaw Questions
library.summary: Naming the defect before reading the choices, decoding the abstract phrasings the credited answer uses, and separating "true of the argument" from "why the argument fails".

spans.text: A flaw question asks you to
describe

what went wrong. It does not ask you to fix it, rebut it, or supply what was missing. That distinction eliminates a whole class of attractive wrong answers: a choice that offers a good objection is answering a weaken question that was not asked. See
Flaw in the Reasoning
Stems in this family:
vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that
the reasoning is flawed because it
questionable because the argument
fails to consider the possibility that

blocks.text: Name it in your own words first

spans.text: The method is one sentence long:
read the argument, say what is wrong with it in plain language, then find the choice that says that in exam language.

This works because the exam's abstractions are hard to evaluate cold. Read five choices phrased as "takes for granted that", "presumes without warrant", "treats a condition as", and all five sound like they might describe something. Read them holding a specific defect you already named, and four fall away instantly.
The vocabulary that makes naming fast is in
The Flaw Catalog
The credited answer describes the defect abstractly. Learning the translations is most of the difficulty.

rows.text: treats a condition that is necessary as one that is sufficient
infers a causal connection from a correlation
draws a conclusion about a whole from evidence about a part
relies on a term used in two different senses
presupposes what it sets out to prove
fails to consider that the reverse may hold

spans.text: Every employee who completed the ethics training reported feeling more confident about compliance. The training is therefore effective at improving compliance.
Name it: the evidence is about
self-reported confidence
, the conclusion is about
actual compliance
. Those are different things, and the argument slides from one to the other.
Now the credited answer is easy to spot:
"treats evidence about employees' perceptions as if it established a fact about their behaviour."
Without the name, that choice competes with four others about sample size, self-selection, and the absence of a control group — all of which are also true of the argument.

blocks.text: "True of the argument" is not the test

spans.text: This is the family's defining trap, and it deserves its own habit.
Every flaw question contains at least one choice that accurately describes something the argument does — it
does
cite an expert, it
does
discuss only one city, it
does
use an example. Accuracy is not the criterion. The criterion is whether that feature is
why the argument fails
Run every surviving choice through both halves:

items.text: Is it true of this argument?
If the argument never does this, eliminate. (Choices describing flaws the argument does not commit are the other half of the distractor set.)
Is it the reason the conclusion does not follow?
If the argument would still fail with this fixed, or would still succeed with it present, eliminate.

spans.text: A choice must pass both. Most wrong answers pass exactly one, which is why they survive a careless read.
Occasionally the defect will not come. Two fallbacks, in order:

items.text: Compare the conclusion's scope to the premises'.
Nine times out of ten the conclusion is broader, stronger, or about a different thing. That mismatch is usually the flaw.
Check for the two most common defects.
Necessary–sufficient confusion and correlation-to-cause account for a large share of the family. Test both explicitly before guessing.
Flaw questions are descriptive: name the defect, do not repair the argument.
Say what is wrong in plain language
Learn the abstract phrasings; matching plain language to abstraction is the real work.
Two-part filter: true of the argument, and the reason it fails. Both, or eliminate.
Stuck? Compare conclusion scope to premise scope, then check necessary–sufficient and causal.

outline.text: Name it in your own words first
"True of the argument" is not the test

library.title: Inference Questions — Must Be True, Most Strongly Supported, Cannot Be True
library.summary: The family with no argument to attack — what follows from the facts, how the three stems differ in strictness, and why the safest-sounding answer usually wins.

spans.text: Inference stimuli usually contain no conclusion at all — they are a set of claims, and the question asks what follows. That changes the whole approach: there is nothing to attack, no gap to bridge, no flaw to name. The task is downward, not sideways. See
Must Be True
Because there is nothing to pre-phrase in the usual sense, this is the one family where going to the choices early is correct. What you
can

do first is combine: if the stimulus contains two conditionals sharing a term, chain them; if it contains two "most" statements about the same group, note the overlap. Frequently the credited answer is exactly that combination.

headers.text: What a good answer looks like

rows.text: Often modest, often a contrapositive or a chain
Can require a small reasonable step
The one choice inconsistent with the facts

spans.text: The difference between the first two is real but narrower than it looks. On
must be true
, any gap disqualifies. On
most strongly supported
, a choice can go slightly beyond the text if nothing else comes close — but "slightly" is doing serious work, and the credited answer is still the most conservative of the plausible ones. See
Most Strongly Supported
Cannot be true
inverts everything: four choices are consistent with the stimulus and one is not. See
Cannot Be True
All of the museum's Renaissance holdings were acquired before 1970. Every work acquired before 1970 was catalogued by hand. Most hand-catalogued works have not yet been digitised.
Chain the conditionals:
Renaissance → acquired before 1970 → hand-catalogued
. So all Renaissance holdings were hand-catalogued.
Now the third fact: most hand-catalogued works are not digitised. Careful — that is about hand-catalogued works
as a whole
, not about the Renaissance subset. "Most Renaissance holdings are not digitised" does
not
follow, because the Renaissance works could all sit in the digitised minority.
What does follow:
"At least some works that were catalogued by hand were acquired before 1970"
— modest, airtight, and exactly the kind of answer this family rewards.
Words like
always
never
only
all
none
must
raise the bar a choice has to clear, and a stimulus of three sentences rarely supports that bar. Words like
some
at least one
may
not all
lower it.

This is a tendency, not a rule — a stimulus containing "all" can license a conclusion containing "all". But when two choices both look defensible, the weaker one is the better bet, and the habit of reaching for the impressive-sounding answer is expensive here.

The classic wrong answer in this family is true, sensible, and one small step beyond the text. The stimulus says a policy reduced emissions; the choice says the policy was worth its cost. Nothing in the stimulus is about cost.

The check: point at the sentence that supports the choice. If you cannot put your finger on specific text, it does not follow — no matter how reasonable it sounds. This is the same discipline that governs Reading Comprehension inference questions; see
Reading Comprehension Question Families

items.text: : conditionals sharing a term, quantifiers about the same group, a numerical constraint.
Combine what combines. Write the chain if there are three or more links.
Go to the choices and eliminate anything requiring information not present.
Among survivors, prefer the one you can support by pointing at text.
No argument to attack — the task is deduction from given facts.
Combine conditionals and quantifiers before reading choices; the answer is often that combination.
Weak, modest answers win more often than strong ones.
Point at the supporting text. If you cannot, the choice does not follow.

library.title: Structure Questions — Main Point, Role, Method, Point at Issue
library.summary: The four questions that ask what a piece of an argument does rather than whether it works, and the descriptive discipline all four share.

spans.text: Structure questions do not ask whether the argument is any good. They ask what it
is
: which sentence is the conclusion, what job a particular sentence does, how the author proceeds, or where two speakers disagree. All four are descriptive, and all four are solved by the analysis in
Argument Anatomy

items.text: The main point of the argument is that…
The statement that X plays which one of the following roles?
The dialogue most supports the claim that they disagree about whether…

spans.text: Run the why-test, then check for the subsidiary-conclusion trap: a claim that has support
and
gives support is not the main point. The main conclusion is the one nothing else in the stimulus is trying to establish.
Two structural tells worth memorising. When a stimulus opens with an attributed view —
"Some economists argue that…"
— the author's conclusion is almost always the rejection that follows. And when a pivot word appears, the conclusion is usually after it.

Credited answers on this subtype are paraphrases, not quotations. A choice that repeats the conclusion verbatim is not automatically right, and one that restates it in different words is not automatically wrong.
You are given one sentence and asked what it does. The workable method is to classify it
before

reading the choices, in three steps: is it the main conclusion, does it support something, or is it supported by something? Then check whether the author endorses it — a claim can be a premise for a view the author is about to reject.

blocks.title: A claim the author does not accept

spans.text: Critics of the transit levy say it will burden low-income households. This concern is not unreasonable: the levy is regressive on its face. But the levy funds free passes for exactly those households, so the net effect is progressive. The levy should pass.
Role of "the levy is regressive on its face": it supports the critics' concern, which the author acknowledges and then overrides. It is
a premise offered in support of a position the author ultimately rejects
— not the conclusion, not a premise for the author's own conclusion, and not an irrelevant aside.
Three of the five choices will describe it as supporting the author's conclusion. It supports the opposing one.
Describe the
technique
, not the content. Common patterns, with their exam phrasing:

items.text: "rejects a generalisation by citing a case that does not conform to it"
"argues that two situations are relevantly similar"
"eliminates competing explanations to establish the remaining one"
"applies a general rule to a particular case"
"shows that a position leads to an untenable consequence"
"draws a distinction between two things that had been treated alike"

spans.text: The credited answer must match on
every
clause. A choice that says "cites statistical evidence to undermine a causal claim" fails if the argument cited an anecdote, even if the rest fits.
Two speakers, and you must find what they actually disagree about. The test is two-sided and both halves are required:
Each speaker must have a position on it, and those positions must conflict.

Most wrong answers fail one half: something only one speaker addressed, or something both mentioned and agreed about. Work by elimination — for each choice, ask "did speaker one take a stance? did speaker two? are they opposed?" — rather than by intuition about the overall tone of the exchange.

Two speakers can sound like they are arguing while agreeing on every proposition, differing only in what they consider important. A choice describing that difference in emphasis is not a point at issue, because neither speaker has denied what the other asserted. Look for a proposition one affirms and the other rejects.

items.text: All four subtypes are descriptive: what the argument is, not whether it works.
Main conclusion: run the why-test and reject subsidiary conclusions.
Role: classify the sentence yourself first, and check whether the author endorses it.
Method: match every clause of the description, including what kind of evidence was used.
Point at issue: both speakers must have taken a stance, and the stances must conflict.

library.title: Numbers, Percentages, and Rates
library.summary: The quantitative traps — rate versus count, shifting bases, composition effects — and why almost every one of them is solved by asking what the denominator did.

blocks.text: The one question that solves most of them

spans.text: When a stimulus mixes a percentage with a count, ask:
what happened to the denominator?

A percentage is a ratio. It can move because the numerator moved, because the denominator moved, or both. An argument that treats a change in rate as a change in count — or the reverse — has ignored the denominator, and that is the flaw. See
Percentage vs. Number

lines: Rate = numerator / denominator
Rate up   + denominator down   → numerator may be unchanged or falling
Rate down + denominator up     → numerator may be unchanged or rising
Count up  + denominator up more → rate falls

items.text: "The share of graduates entering public-interest law doubled, so more graduates are entering public-interest law."
Only if the class size held steady. If the class halved, the count is flat.
"More residents were treated for asthma this year, so asthma is more prevalent."
Only if the population held steady.
A hospital with a higher mortality
may be taking the harder cases. Rates across differently-composed groups compare the groups' composition as much as their performance.
Composition shift (the average that moved without anyone moving).
The average changes because the mix changed. This one is subtle enough to earn its own example.

blocks.title: The average that moved without anyone moving

spans.text: The average tenure of employees at the firm fell from nine years to six over the past year. Retention must be deteriorating.
Ask what happened to the denominator — here, who is in the pool. Suppose the firm hired forty new people and nobody left. Every existing employee's tenure went
up
by a year, and the average still fell sharply, because the pool now contains forty people with tenure near zero.
The conclusion does not follow, and the flaw is a composition shift, not bad arithmetic. A weaken choice reading
"the firm expanded its workforce by 40% during the year"
is the credited answer.
Quantitative traps rarely appear as their own question type. They arrive inside other families:

items.text: "treats a change in proportion as though it established a change in absolute number."
of a paradox — two facts that conflict until you notice one is a rate and the other a count. See
in a causal argument, by showing the base population changed. See

spans.text: The exam is careful with its quantitative vocabulary, and so should you be.

rows.text: A summary of a distribution, sensitive to composition
A ratio of ratios — says nothing about either absolute risk

spans.text: That last row matters. "Twice as likely" is compatible with a risk moving from one in a million to two in a million. A conclusion about how many people are affected does not follow from a relative risk.

The stimulus almost never tells you what the denominator did. That silence is the point — the argument needs the base to be stable and does not say so, which makes "the population was unchanged" a classic unstated assumption. On assumption questions with a statistical stimulus, check for exactly that choice; see
The Assumption Family

items.text: Ask what the denominator did. It solves most of the family.
Rates and counts do not imply each other unless the base is stable.
Rate comparisons across differently-composed groups compare composition too.
An average can move sharply with no individual changing — composition shifts.
Relative risk says nothing about absolute numbers; "twice as likely" can be tiny either way.

outline.text: The one question that solves most of them

library.title: Paradox and Evaluate
library.summary: Reconciling two facts that seem to conflict, and identifying the question whose answer would settle an argument — two families that reward the same "what would change my mind" instinct.

spans.text: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?
The stimulus presents two facts that sit uncomfortably together. Your job is to add a third fact that makes both comfortable —
not
to deny either one. See
Resolve the Paradox
The single most useful habit:
state the tension in one sentence before reading the choices.

"Sales rose while the number of customers fell" or "the drug worked in the lab and failed in the field". Once the tension is named, the credited answer is usually the one obvious thing that would explain it.
The exam reuses a small set of explanations:

items.text: The two facts are about different populations that were treated as one.
The average moved because the mix changed, not because any individual did.
A percentage and an absolute number moved in opposite directions because the base changed. See
Both facts are true because something else intervened between them.
The two measurements cover different periods, or one lags the other.

spans.text: Since the hospital introduced its rapid-triage protocol, the average time from arrival to treatment has increased by eleven minutes. Yet patient outcomes have improved substantially, and the protocol is widely credited for the improvement.
Tension in one sentence:
waiting longer, but doing better.

Now generate: perhaps the protocol identifies low-urgency patients and deliberately delays them, so the average rose while the urgent cases are seen faster. That is a composition explanation, and a choice reading
"the protocol routes non-urgent patients to a separate queue, reducing the wait for critical cases"
resolves it exactly.
Note what does
not
resolve it: a choice arguing outcomes did not really improve. That denies a premise, which is never the job here.
Half the wrong answers in this family make the discrepancy
worse

— they explain why one of the two facts is even more surprising than it looked. Under time pressure these read as "relevant" and get picked. After choosing, reread the two facts with your answer inserted and ask whether they now sit comfortably. If you still feel the tension, you picked a deepener.
Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?
You are not strengthening or weakening. You are naming the
question whose answer decides the case
. See
Evaluate the Argument
The mechanical tool is the
variance test
. For each choice, imagine the two extreme answers:

items.text: ), does the argument get notably stronger?

spans.text: A choice passes only if both directions move the argument, and in opposite directions. A choice whose answer leaves the argument unchanged either way is the standard distractor, no matter how on-topic it sounds.

lines: Argument: the new fertiliser caused the yield increase.
Choice:   "Whether neighbouring farms that did not use the fertiliser
saw similar yield increases."
Yes → neighbours also gained → alternative cause → argument weakens
No  → only treated farms gained            → argument strengthens
Both directions move it. Passes.

spans.text: Because evaluate questions are usually built on causal stimuli, the variance test almost always lands on one of the four attacks in
Causal Reasoning
— most often ruling an alternative cause in or out.

items.text: Paradox: both stated facts are true. Add a third that reconciles them; never deny one.
Name the tension in one sentence before reading the choices.
Standard resolutions: hidden group, composition change, rate versus count, different mechanism, timing.
Evaluate: find the question whose answer decides the argument, using the variance test.
A choice that leaves the argument unchanged either way fails, however relevant it sounds.

library.title: Parallel Reasoning and Parallel Flaw
library.summary: The most time-expensive family on the section — how to abstract an argument to its skeleton, what has to match, and when to skip.

spans.text: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
You are matching
structure
, and structure means four things:

items.text: — conditional chain, causal claim, generalisation from a sample, analogy.
— a prediction matches a prediction, a recommendation matches a recommendation, a claim of fact matches a claim of fact.
. A stimulus concluding "may well be" does not match a choice concluding "certainly is".
— a valid argument matches a valid one; an invalid argument matches one that fails

spans.text: What does
not
have to match: subject matter. In fact the exam deliberately changes the topic, and choices that keep the stimulus's topic are usually traps. See
Parallel Reasoning

blocks.text: Abstract before you read the choices

spans.text: Reduce the stimulus to a skeleton using letters. This is not optional decoration — it is the only way to compare six arguments without rereading each one three times.

lines: Stimulus: Every accredited programme requires a clinical year.
Fairhaven does not require a clinical year.
So Fairhaven is not accredited.
Skeleton: All A are B.  X is not B.  Therefore X is not A.
(valid — contrapositive)

spans.text: Now scan the choices for that shape. Any choice concluding "X is not A" from "X is not B" where the rule ran
A → B
matches. A choice concluding "X is A" because "X is B" is affirming the consequent — a different, invalid form.
Stimulus: Most of the firm's successful appeals were argued by senior partners. Novak is a senior partner. So Novak has probably argued a successful appeal.
Skeleton:
Most A are B. X is B. Therefore X is probably A.
The flaw is a reversal of a "most" statement — most successes came from senior partners, which says nothing about what share of senior partners produced a success. See
Quantifiers
The credited choice will run the same reversal on a different topic:
"Most of the museum's stolen works were taken at night. This vase was taken at night. So it was probably one of the stolen works."
Same defect, same "probably", different subject.
A choice with a genuine flaw of a different kind — say a causal reversal — does not match, however wrong it is.
Same procedure, one addition:
name the flaw first
, using
The Flaw Catalog
. Then find the choice that commits
that
defect. A choice that is flawed differently is wrong, and the exam always supplies two or three of them.
The most common near-miss: a choice with the right topic-shape but a different error, or a choice that is valid when the stimulus was flawed. Checking validity explicitly catches both.

A choice about the same subject as the stimulus — both about hospitals, both about universities — is a deliberate lure. Topic similarity is evidence of nothing. Cover the nouns with letters and the resemblance evaporates.
Parallel questions are the most time-expensive on the section: six arguments to analyse instead of one. If you are behind pace, they are the correct thing to leave.
The practical rule from
Pacing

: if a parallel question appears while you are behind, mark a letter, flag it, and return only if time remains. Two ordinary questions answered carefully are worth more than one parallel question answered in four minutes.
Before doing any structural work, read only the
last sentence
of each choice. Conclusion type and strength eliminate two or three choices in under fifteen seconds, and you only have to abstract the survivors.

items.text: Match logical form, conclusion type, language strength, and validity — never subject matter.
Abstract the stimulus to letters before touching the choices.
On parallel flaw, name the defect first, then find the choice committing that same defect.
Same-topic choices are lures; cover the nouns.
Highest time cost on the section — the correct question to skip when behind.

outline.text: Abstract before you read the choices

library.title: Principle Questions
library.summary: Moving between abstract rules and concrete cases in both directions, and the conditional structure hiding inside almost every principle.

spans.text: A principle is a general rule. Principle questions move between the rule and a case, and the stem tells you which direction. See
Principle Application

items.text: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?
You are given a case and asked for the rule that licenses it.
Which one of the following judgements most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
You are given a rule and asked which case it governs.

spans.text: A third variant appears occasionally: two principles are stated and you must find the case they jointly decide, or the case where they conflict.
This is the whole technique. A principle says:
when these conditions hold, this follows.
Rewrite it in the notation from
Conditional Logic
and the question becomes mechanical.

lines: Principle: "A public official should recuse herself from any decision
in which she has a personal financial interest."
Notation:  Personal financial interest → Should recuse

spans.text: Now the direction of the stem tells you what to check.

items.text: the principle means the case must satisfy the
condition. A case where the official has a financial interest is governed. A case where she recused herself is
governed — that is the necessary condition, and satisfying it triggers nothing.
a conclusion means the principle's sufficient condition must be met by the facts and its necessary condition must be what the argument concluded.

spans.text: Principle: A reviewer should disclose any relationship with an author whose work she evaluates.
Notation:
Relationship with author → Should disclose
Conforms:
Chen evaluates a manuscript by a former colleague and discloses the connection. Sufficient condition met, necessary condition satisfied.
Does not conform, and is the standard trap:
Okonjo discloses that she has no relationship with the author she is reviewing. She has satisfied the
necessary

condition without the sufficient one triggering. The principle says nothing about her case, so it neither approves nor forbids what she did — and a choice describing it as conforming is testing whether you reversed the arrow.
The credited answer matches the principle on every dimension, and the exam builds distractors by shifting one:

items.text: does not decide a case about a private contractor.
— a principle qualified with "ordinarily" cannot decide a case conclusively.

spans.text: Principle questions often involve conduct, and one choice usually describes behaviour that is clearly right or clearly wrong. That choice is frequently not governed by the stated principle at all.
The test is not "was this person's conduct appropriate" but "does
this rule
decide
this case
". A principle can be silent about genuinely bad behaviour, and when it is, the choice is wrong.
On the identify direction, treat the question as a sufficient-assumption problem in disguise — see
The Assumption Family
. Find the gap between the facts and the judgement, and choose the principle that bridges exactly that gap.
The common error is choosing a principle that is
too broad

. A rule that would justify the conclusion and a hundred other things is still sufficient, so breadth alone is not disqualifying — but a rule broad enough to be obviously false, or one whose sufficient condition the facts never establish, is. Check both halves: does the case trigger it, and does it deliver the conclusion?

items.text: Rewrite every principle as a conditional before doing anything else.
Applying: the case must meet the sufficient condition. Meeting the necessary one triggers nothing.
Justifying: treat it as a sufficient assumption — bridge the gap between facts and judgement.
Match on who, what, and how strongly; distractors shift exactly one of those.
The question is whether the rule decides the case, not whether the conduct was admirable.

library.title: Logical Reasoning — Section Guide
library.summary: What the two scored LR sections demand, the family map that organises every question type, and the four-step routine that works on all of them.

spans.text: Two scored 35-minute sections, roughly 25 questions each. Each question is a short stimulus — usually 30 to 90 words — followed by one stem and five choices. Because both scored LR sections count, this section is close to half your score, and it is where a study plan should concentrate. See
How the LSAT Is Built

Question difficulty is not uniform and is loosely ordered: the first eight or so are typically approachable, questions ten through twenty carry the weight, and the last few are often the hardest on the section. That ordering is what makes triage possible; see
Pacing
Every LR question belongs to one of seven families, and the family determines the method. Learn to classify from the stem before reading anything else.

rows.text: Supplies an unstated link the argument needs
Adds a new fact that helps or hurts the inference
vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that
Names the defect in the reasoning
Follows from the stimulus without adding anything
Describes what a part of the argument does
Reconciles two facts, or identifies a decisive test
Matches an abstract pattern to a concrete case

spans.text: Each family has its own article:
The Assumption Family
Strengthen and Weaken
Flaw Questions
Inference Questions
Structure Questions
Paradox and Evaluate
Parallel Reasoning and Parallel Flaw
Principle Questions
The same routine works across every family, and running it in order is what separates consistent scorers from streaky ones.

items.text: Ten words tell you what job to do, and reading the stimulus without knowing the job means reading it twice.
Find the conclusion, mark the support, notice the pivot. Not for content — for shape. See
Say what the answer must accomplish, in your own words, before looking. On assumption, strengthen, weaken and flaw questions this is worth more than any elimination technique.

blocks.title: The routine on a hard item

spans.text: Stem: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

Stimulus: A recent audit found that departments using the new procurement software processed invoices 40% faster than departments still using the old system. The software vendor concludes that adopting the software will reduce processing times across the entire agency.
Step 1:
flaw question — I need the defect, not a rebuttal.
Step 2:
conclusion is "adopting the software will reduce processing times agency-wide"; support is a 40% gap between departments that already chose it and those that did not.
Step 3:
pre-phrase — the departments that adopted early may differ from the rest in ways that explain the speed. Self-selection. The argument assumes the comparison groups are alike.
Step 4:
now scan for
"takes for granted that departments that adopted the software are representative of the agency as a whole"
and ignore the four choices about cost, training, and vendor bias.

items.text: The subject matter is irrelevant. What matters is which sentence supports which.
Skipping the pre-phrase under time pressure.
This is exactly backwards: the pre-phrase is a time
, because it makes four choices obviously wrong at a glance.
Answering a weaken question with a flaw answer is a specific, common, avoidable error.
Rereading the stimulus for each choice.
If you need the stimulus five times you did not extract its structure the first time.

blocks.title: Answering the argument instead of the question

spans.text: A stimulus makes a claim you find unconvincing, and a choice says something you agree with about why. That is not the question. Every stem defines a narrow job — supply the assumption, name the defect, add a fact that weakens. Agreement is not the criterion; doing the stated job is. This one habit accounts for a large fraction of missed LR questions at every score level.

items.text: Two scored sections, roughly half the exam. Concentrate study time here.
Seven families; classify from the stem before reading the stimulus.
Stem, structure, pre-phrase, eliminate — in that order, every time.
Difficulty rises through the section, which is what makes triage viable.
The commonest error is doing a reasonable thing that the stem did not ask for.

library.title: Strengthen and Weaken
library.summary: How to attack and defend an inference without touching the premises, the causal template that covers most of the family, and the degree language that decides close calls.

spans.text: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
You are handed a new fact and asked whether it makes the conclusion harder or easier to accept. Two constraints follow, and almost every miss in this family violates one of them.
You accept the premises.
A choice that denies a stated fact is attacking the wrong thing. The argument's vulnerability lives in the
move
from premises to conclusion. See
Weaken Question
You attack the specific conclusion.

Not the topic, not the author's politics, not a related claim. If the conclusion is "the programme should be expanded", a fact showing the programme is expensive weakens only if cost bears on the stated reasoning.
The large majority of strengthen and weaken stimuli are causal, and
Causal Reasoning
gives the four attacks. Applied here:

rows.text: Establish that the cause preceded the effect
Show the comparison group was controlled
Show the cause without the effect
Show the effect tracks the cause across cases

spans.text: Pre-phrasing from this table before reading the choices is the single most effective habit in the family. You will frequently find you predicted the credited answer almost word for word.
Since the county introduced its mandatory recycling programme, household waste sent to landfill has fallen by 22%. The programme is clearly working.

Before reading choices, generate: (a) something else changed at the same time — a new landfill fee, a large employer leaving town; (b) waste is being diverted somewhere other than recycling, such as illegal dumping; (c) the 22% is a rate and the population shrank.
A choice reading
"During the same period, the county began charging households by the bag for landfill collection"
is attack (a) — an alternative cause. That is the credited answer, and you had it before you read a word of the choices.
Not every stimulus is causal. The other common shapes:

items.text: Weaken by showing the two cases differ in a relevant respect; strengthen by showing they are alike where it matters.
Argument from a sample or survey.
Weaken by attacking representativeness, response rates, or self-reporting. See
Weaken by showing the plan will not achieve its goal, will cost more than it saves, or has a side effect that defeats the purpose. Strengthen by ruling those out.
Weaken by identifying a condition that has changed since the trend was observed.

spans.text: When two choices both point the right direction, strength settles it. On weaken questions, "some evidence suggests" loses to "in every documented case"; on strengthen questions, a choice that eliminates a possibility outright beats one that makes it less likely.
But strength only matters
after
relevance. A very strong statement about something the conclusion does not depend on does nothing, and the exam builds distractors exactly there: forceful language attached to an irrelevant claim.
A choice damages a subsidiary claim, an example the author used, or the author's credibility — and leaves the main conclusion untouched. It genuinely weakens
something
, which is why it survives elimination.
The check is mechanical: state the main conclusion aloud, then ask whether this choice makes
that sentence
less likely. If you have to route through two inferences to explain how, it is probably the trap.
Take any causal weaken item, such as

, and after answering, write the strengthener for the same argument. Forcing yourself to produce both makes the four-attack structure automatic, and strengthen questions stop feeling like a separate skill.

items.text: Accept the premises; attack or defend the inference to the stated conclusion.
Most stimuli are causal — pre-phrase from the four attacks before reading choices.
Non-causal shapes: analogy, sample, plan, prediction, each with its own weak point.
Relevance first, then degree. Strong language on an irrelevant claim does nothing.
Beware the choice that weakens a subsidiary point and leaves the conclusion standing.

library.title: How the LSAT Is Built
library.summary: The shape of the exam — which sections are scored, how long each runs, where the unscored section hides, and what the whole thing is actually measuring.

spans.text: The LSAT does not test law. It tests four narrow abilities that law school assumes you already have: reading dense prose for structure rather than for facts, evaluating whether a conclusion actually follows from what preceded it, holding a set of formal constraints in your head while you draw consequences from them, and writing a position you can defend under time pressure.
That framing matters more than it sounds. Almost every wrong answer a beginner picks is
true
, or
plausible
, or
something the passage would probably agree with
. Almost none of them do the specific job the question asked for. The exam is a test of task discipline as much as of reasoning, and every technique in this library is downstream of that one fact.
A scored administration is four 35-minute sections plus a separately-delivered writing sample. Three of the four count toward your score; one does not.

rows.text: An extra LR or RC section being pretested

spans.text: Two consequences follow immediately. First,
Logical Reasoning is roughly half your score

— two of the three scored sections. A point of LR improvement is worth about twice a point of RC improvement, which is why a study plan that splits time evenly between them is already misallocated. Second,
you cannot identify the unscored section while you are taking it
, and people who try are reliably wrong. Treat all four as scored; the alternative is throwing away a scored section on a hunch.

A test taker sits two Logical Reasoning sections and decides the second one "felt like a pretest" because the questions seemed strange. They coast through it at half effort. The strange-feeling section was scored; the ordinary-feeling first one was the pretest. They have just discarded a quarter of their exam on a feeling.
There is no tell. The only correct policy is to treat every section as the one that counts.

Logic Games — formally Analytical Reasoning — was removed from the scored exam in August 2024. It survives in this library and in the drill bank as a reasoning trainer, not as a scored section: the constraint-tracking it teaches transfers directly to conditional questions in Logical Reasoning, and the boards are the cleanest available practice at holding several rules in working memory at once. See
Logic Games
for how to use it now that it no longer counts.
The clock is the exam's real difficulty. Every section is written so that a careful, unhurried reader would score near the top and almost nobody has time to be one.

items.text: gives you about 1 minute 25 seconds per question, and the questions are not equally hard. The skill is not "go faster" but "spend 45 seconds on the easy ones so you can spend two and a half minutes on the hard ones". See

gives you roughly 8 minutes 45 seconds per passage set, of which 3 to 4 minutes is reading and the rest is answering. Readers who try to memorise the passage run out of time on the questions; readers who skim have to re-read for every question. See
is untimed in the sense that nobody scores it out of a hundred, and completely load-bearing in the sense that schools read it and an unsubmitted sample makes your file incomplete. See

spans.text: Knowing what is
out of scope
prevents a large class of wrong answers.

items.text: If an answer requires a fact from your own life, it is wrong. The passage or stimulus supplies everything.
A stimulus can assert something false. Your job is what follows
Comprehension per minute beats words per minute on every measured section.
Nothing on the exam requires knowing a single case, rule, or statute.

spans.text: The most common wrong answer on the entire exam is the choice that is reasonable, sensible, and something a thoughtful person would agree with — and that does not do what the question asked. "Which one most weakens the argument" is not "which one sounds like a good objection". Discipline about the question stem is the single highest-return habit available;
Answer-Choice Elimination
is built around it.

items.text: Four 35-minute sections; three scored, one unscored and unidentifiable. Treat all four as real.
Logical Reasoning is two of the three scored sections — roughly half the score, and where study time should concentrate.
The exam tests task discipline under a clock, not knowledge; every section is doable untimed.
Logic Games left the scored exam in August 2024 but remains the best available trainer for constraint tracking.
Wrong answers are usually plausible. Right answers do exactly what the stem asked.

library.title: Scoring, Scaling, and What a Point Is Worth
library.summary: How raw answers become a 120–180 score, why the curve is not a curve, and where on the scale a single extra question changes the most.

spans.text: Your
raw score

is the number of questions you answered correctly across the three scored sections — roughly 75 to 77 of them. Nothing is subtracted for a wrong answer. That single fact has a strategic consequence bigger than most people give it:
there is never a reason to leave a bubble empty
. See
Triage and Guessing
The raw score is then converted to a
scaled score

from 120 to 180 using a conversion table built for that specific exam form. The table is set before anyone sits the exam, by pretesting questions in the unscored variable section. This is why "the curve" is a misnomer — you are not competing against the people in the room with you. An easier form needs more raw points for the same scaled score; a harder form needs fewer. The conversion is a difficulty adjustment, not a ranking.

blocks.text: The scale is not evenly spaced

spans.text: Percentiles are what schools actually read, and they are wildly non-linear. The distribution bunches in the middle, so the same one-question improvement buys very different amounts depending on where you start.

headers.text: Roughly what one extra point moves

spans.text: Percentiles shift year to year and LSAC publishes the current table; the shape, not the exact figures, is what to plan around.

Two test takers each find three more correct answers through a month of work. The first moves from 149 to 152 and climbs roughly nine percentile points — a different admissions conversation. The second moves from 172 to 175 and climbs about one. Same work, very different return.

This is not an argument against high scorers improving. It is an argument for knowing which curve you are on, and for a mid-scorer to expect visible returns rather than assuming the exam is immovable.

blocks.text: What this means for how you study

items.text: , the fastest points are usually not in exotic question types. They are in finishing sections you currently do not finish, and in the easy questions you rush past to reach hard ones you were never going to get. Read
, the profile is usually uneven: one section, or two or three question families, carries almost all the loss. An error log makes that visible in a week; see
, remaining misses are typically single hard items per section, and the work shifts from method to precision — the discipline in

spans.text: Scaled scores across different practice forms are not directly comparable, and the noise between two forms can exceed a month of real improvement. Track
raw correct per section
over time. It is the number that actually moves, and it tells you
where
it moved.

A single administration has measurement error of roughly plus or minus three points. Two people whose scores differ by two points are, statistically, indistinguishable. Treat your result as a band rather than a value: a 164 means "roughly 161 to 167", and a practice test that comes back four points below your average is inside normal variance rather than evidence that something broke.
The practical version of this: never rewrite a study plan on one practice test. Change it on a trend of three.

items.text: No penalty for wrong answers, so every bubble gets filled — always.
Scaled scores come from a per-form conversion table set in advance; you are not graded against the room.
Percentiles are non-linear: a point is worth several times more in the low 150s than above 170.
Track raw correct per section, not scaled scores, to see real movement.
One administration carries roughly plus or minus three points of measurement error. Read scores as bands.

outline.text: The scale is not evenly spaced
What this means for how you study

library.title: Pacing
library.summary: Why uniform pacing is the wrong target, the checkpoint system that replaces it, and how to spend unequal time on unequal questions.

blocks.text: Uniform pacing is the wrong target

spans.text: "About 1 minute 25 per Logical Reasoning question" is an average, and treating it as a budget is the mistake that defines mid-range scores. The questions are not equally hard and are loosely ordered by difficulty, so spending equal time on each guarantees you overspend on the easy ones and underspend on the hard ones.
The correct target is
unequal

: 45 to 60 seconds on early questions, 90 seconds on the middle, and two to three minutes available for the handful of genuinely hard items late in the section. The time for the hard ones is bought from the easy ones, and it can only be bought there.

rows.text: Easier by design; this is where time is banked
Hardest items; needs the banked time

spans.text: Checking the clock after every question is a tax on attention and produces anxiety without information. Use two or three
checkpoints
instead.
For a 25-question Logical Reasoning section starting at 35:00:
For Reading Comprehension:

At a checkpoint you do exactly one thing: compare, and if you are behind, change behaviour immediately rather than resolving to go faster. "Going faster" is not an action. Skipping the next long question is.
You reach question 10 with 20 minutes left instead of 24. You are four minutes behind, with fifteen questions to go.
Wrong response: read faster and try to make it up gradually. This produces rushed reading on the hardest part of the section and typically loses more than the four minutes.

Right response: buy the time back in one transaction. Scan questions 11 to 15 and find the one longest stimulus or the one parallel-reasoning item. Guess it, flag it, move on. You have recovered two to three minutes in twenty seconds, and you spend the rest of the section at proper speed instead of rushing fifteen questions.
Some test takers do better with a deliberate two-pass structure, especially in Logical Reasoning.
First pass:
answer everything you can do at normal speed. When a question resists — you have read the stimulus twice and have no pre-phrase — mark a letter, flag it, and move on. Do not linger.
Second pass:
return to the flagged questions with whatever time remains, hardest last.

The advantage is that no easy question at the end of the section goes unseen because a hard question in the middle ate the clock. The cost is the overhead of returning. It suits people whose error log shows late-section questions missed for lack of time rather than lack of method — see
The Error Log
You have spent ninety seconds on a question and have it down to two choices. Every additional thirty seconds feels justified because you are so close.

You are not close. Down-to-two after ninety seconds means the distinction is subtle, and subtle distinctions rarely resolve through staring. Guessing between two choices is a 50% shot that costs zero further seconds; continuing is a maybe-70% shot that costs sixty and takes them from a question you would have answered correctly.
The rule that beats intuition:
when you notice you have spent too long, you already have.
Choose between the survivors, flag it, move.
Pacing is trained, not decided. Three stages:

items.text: There is no point pacing a method you do not have.
— 40 minutes for a 35-minute section — until accuracy holds.
, with checkpoints, until the checkpoint numbers stop surprising you.

spans.text: Skipping to stage three is the standard mistake and produces a stable habit of rushing.

items.text: Target unequal times: bank seconds on early questions to spend on late ones.
Use two or three checkpoints, not a per-question stopwatch.
Behind at a checkpoint? Buy the time back in one transaction by skipping a long question.
The sunk-cost minute is the biggest single leak; when you notice, you are already over.
Train pace in three stages — untimed, generous, real. Skipping stages trains rushing.

outline.text: Uniform pacing is the wrong target

library.title: Quantifiers — All, Most, Some, and What Combines
library.summary: The three quantifiers, what each one licenses, which pairs combine into a valid inference, and why "most" plus "most" is the exam's favourite overlap question.

items.text: — every member, no exceptions. Equivalent to a conditional:
— more than half. On the exam this means strictly greater than 50%, and it includes "all" as a special case: if all A are B, then most A are B is also true.
— at least one. This is the quantifier people get wrong, because ordinary English uses "some" to mean "a few but not all". On the exam
some means one or more, up to and including every single one

spans.text: That last point matters constantly. "Some senators voted for the bill" is true if all one hundred did. An answer choice saying "some A are B" is not contradicted by evidence that all A are B.

blocks.text: What reverses and what does not

spans.text: Some

and its negation-free relatives are symmetric. If some A are B, then some B are A — at least one thing is both, and which side you look from does not change that. The same is true of "no": if no A are B, then no B are A.
All
and
most
are not symmetric.
All A are B
tells you nothing about how much of B is A.
Most A are B
likewise: most surgeons are university graduates, but almost no university graduates are surgeons.
This is the whole content of the topic. Two quantified statements sharing a common term either license an inference or they do not.
Two rows deserve attention.
Most + most sharing the
sufficient
term gives you
some

* If most of the firm's partners are litigators and most of the firm's partners went to state schools, the two majorities must overlap by at least one person — you cannot have two groups each larger than half of the same set that share no member. So some litigators went to state schools. This is the exam's favourite overlap inference.
Most + most sharing the
middle
term gives you nothing.
* Most A are B, most B are C — the As could sit entirely in the part of B that is not C. No inference.

blocks.title: The overlap inference in the wild

spans.text: Most of the applicants who were interviewed had prior clerkship experience. Most of the applicants who were interviewed submitted a writing sample.
Both "most" statements are about the same set — applicants who were interviewed. Two subsets each larger than half must intersect.
Credited inference:
at least one interviewed applicant had both clerkship experience and a writing sample.
Anything stronger — "most had both", "everyone with clerkship experience submitted a sample" — overreaches and is a distractor. Try it against
Inference and flaw questions both reward being able to negate cleanly.

items.text: — not "no A are B", which is far stronger.
at most half of A are B

spans.text: Over-negating is the standard error: people flip "all" to "none" and then evaluate an answer that was never on the table. The same discipline powers the negation test in
The Assumption Family

A stimulus says some board members opposed the merger. A choice says all board members opposed it. Beginners eliminate the choice as contradicted — but "some" is silent about whether all did, so the choice is
unsupported
, not
contradicted
. On a must-be-true question that distinction is invisible. On a cannot-be-true or a most-strongly-supported question it decides the item. See
Cannot Be True

items.text: Some means at least one, up to and including all. It never implies "not all".
Some and no are symmetric; all and most are not.
Most plus most on a shared sufficient term yields some. On a shared middle term it yields nothing.
All chains with all; most chains forward through all, never backward.
Negate precisely: not-all is some-are-not, not none.

outline.text: What reverses and what does not

library.title: Comparative Passages
library.summary: The two-passage set — how to map the relationship rather than each text, and the agreement, disagreement and role questions that only appear here.

spans.text: One of the four sets each section is comparative: two shorter passages, A and B, on a shared topic, followed by questions that are mostly about the
relationship
between them. See
Comparative Passages
The reading is not harder. The mistake is treating it as two ordinary passages and mapping each in isolation, which produces two good maps and no answer to the questions that actually appear.
After reading both, you want four things:

items.text: Does B respond to A, extend it, illustrate it, narrow it, or address the same topic independently?
What does one assert that the other denies?

lines: A:   Municipal charters spread through trade networks.
B:   Charters spread through ecclesiastical administration.
Rel: Independent competing explanations of the same pattern;
B does not mention A.
Agree:   the pattern is uneven; regional variation is real.
Disagree: which mechanism is primary.
Scope:   A covers 1100–1300; B covers 1150–1250 only.

spans.text: That last line matters more than it looks. Comparative passages frequently differ in
scope
— one broader, one narrower, one general and one a case study — and scope differences are a common credited answer to relationship questions.

rows.text: B names or clearly targets A's position
Same framework, new application or later period
Same topic, no engagement, possibly compatible
A is theoretical, B is a concrete case

spans.text: Passages that never mention each other are the norm, not the exception. "B rebuts A" is over-selected by test takers and is correct less often than it feels.

blocks.text: The question types unique to this set

items.text: Requires each passage to support the claim. A statement only A makes fails, even if B would probably accept it —
. This is the same two-sided discipline as point-at-issue in
Both must take a position, and the positions must conflict.
Passage B relates to Passage A in that…
The relationship map answers it directly.
A term used in both passages…
Frequently the two authors use the same word differently, and the question is testing exactly that.

spans.text: A argues that expanding public transit reduces urban emissions and should be funded through congestion charges. B argues that transit expansion reduces emissions only when paired with parking restrictions, and is silent on funding.
"Both authors would agree that transit expansion can reduce emissions"
— supported. A asserts it; B asserts it conditionally, which still commits B to the "can".
"Both authors would agree that congestion charges are the appropriate funding mechanism"
