— not supported. B never addresses funding. Silence is not agreement, and this is the family's characteristic trap.
"The authors disagree about whether transit expansion reduces emissions"
— false. They disagree about the conditions, not the effect.

The most frequent error on comparative sets is inferring one author's position on a topic the other raised. If Passage B never discusses funding, B has no position on funding, and no choice about B's view of funding can be supported.
Before selecting an agreement or disagreement answer, locate the supporting text in
both
passages. If you can only point to one, eliminate.

Read A, map it in one line, read B, map it in one line, then spend fifteen seconds on the relationship before touching the questions. Do not read both and then try to reconstruct — the relationship is what the set is about, and building it while B is fresh is much faster than rebuilding it later.

items.text: Map the relationship, not two separate passages.
Record: each claim, the relationship type, agreements, disagreements, and scope differences.
Passages that never engage each other are the norm; "B rebuts A" is over-selected.
Agreement and disagreement questions need supporting text in
Silence is not assent — the single most common trap in the set.

outline.text: The question types unique to this set

library.title: Passage Mapping
library.summary: The four-line map that replaces re-reading — what to record per paragraph, what to mark in the margin, and the structural patterns most passages follow.

spans.text: A map is not notes. Notes record content; a map records
function
. For each paragraph you want one short phrase answering "what is this paragraph
doing
", plus a mark showing whose view it carries.

lines: ¶1  problem + traditional answer
¶2  evidence for traditional answer
¶3  PIVOT — new evidence undercuts it
¶4  AUTHOR: revised account, concedes ¶2 data

spans.text: Four lines, written or held in your head, produced during a single read. That map is what makes the section open-book in practice rather than in theory. See
Passage Structure

blocks.text: What to mark as you read

spans.text: Keep annotation minimal — heavy underlining is re-reading in disguise. Four marks cover almost everything:

items.text: . These are where structure turns, and questions cluster around them.
— marks where the author stops reporting and starts judging. This is the most valuable thing in the passage.

spans.text: Do not mark: names, dates, technical terms, statistics. You can find those in seconds when a question asks, and marking them costs attention you need for structure.
Most passages follow one of a handful of structures. Recognising which one you are in after the first paragraph accelerates everything after.

rows.text: ¶1 states an accepted account, a pivot arrives
Two or three theories presented in turn
A difficulty is set out, an approach offered
A person or text and its reputation
A concept, then its application or consequence

spans.text: A passage on why certain medieval towns adopted written charters:

lines: ¶1  Phenomenon: charters spread unevenly across regions.
¶2  Explanation A — trade volume. Presented, some support.
¶3  Explanation B — proximity to episcopal courts. Stronger
evidence cited.
¶4  AUTHOR: B is better supported but A is not eliminated;
the two may interact. Tone: measured, favours B.

spans.text: Predict the questions before reading them. There will be a main-point question (answer: B better explains the pattern, though A retains some force), an attitude question (measured endorsement of B, not dismissal of A), a detail question about the evidence in ¶3, and at least one trap answer that overstates the author's rejection of A.
That prediction is worth roughly a minute across the set.
Attitude questions are decided by
degree
, and the exam scores the difference between "critical" and "dismissive". Calibrate:

items.text: the author reports without evaluating. This is common and under-selected.

spans.text: Most LSAT authors are qualified, not strong. An answer choice using an extreme word is usually wrong for that reason alone. See
Tone

A map that reads "¶2: sales figures, 1847, low reviews" is notes, and it will not help you. The same paragraph mapped as "¶2: evidence for the traditional view" answers structure questions, tells you where to look for the sales figures, and takes fewer words.
If your map contains a proper noun, you are probably recording content.

items.text: Map function, not content: one phrase per paragraph plus whose view it carries.
Mark pivots, attribution shifts, evaluative language, and lists. Nothing else.
Recognise the passage shape early; it predicts where the author stands.
Calibrate attitude by degree — most authors are qualified, and extreme choices are usually wrong.
Predicting the question set from the map is worth about a minute per passage.

outline.text: What to mark as you read

library.title: Reading Comprehension Question Families
library.summary: Global, detail, inference, function, attitude, phrase-in-context and analogy questions — what each demands and where each is answered from.

spans.text: The main point of the passage is…
The passage is primarily concerned with…
Answered from the
map
, not from any sentence. The credited answer covers the whole passage — including the pivot — at the right level of generality. See
Main Point Question

Two failure modes: a choice that describes only one paragraph (too narrow) and a choice that describes the general topic without the author's angle (too broad). If the passage argued that a traditional view is incomplete, "the history of a traditional view" is too broad and "the sales figures for an 1847 treatise" is too narrow.
According to the passage…
The passage states that…
Answered by
going back and reading the sentence

. These are the most reliably gettable questions in the section and the most commonly missed through overconfidence. The credited answer is a paraphrase of something explicitly stated; a choice that is true, sensible, and not stated is wrong. See
Detail Question
The passage suggests that…
It can be inferred from the passage that…
The author would most likely agree that…
The standard is what the passage
supports
, which is stricter than what it fails to contradict and looser than what it says outright. See
RC Inference
The reliable check is the same one from
Inference Questions
: point at the text. If you cannot identify a sentence or two doing the supporting, the choice does not follow, however reasonable it sounds.
Text: "Although the charters were drafted in Latin, surviving marginalia suggest that town clerks routinely glossed key provisions in the vernacular for the benefit of councillors."
Supported:
at least some councillors could not read Latin fluently. The gloss existed for their benefit; that is what the sentence is for.
Not supported, and attractive:
the councillors were illiterate. Nothing here says that — glossing Latin into the vernacular tells you about Latin, not about literacy.
Not supported:
the charters were unpopular. The sentence is silent on reception entirely.
The author mentions the sales figures primarily in order to…
The second paragraph serves to…
Answered from the
map
. The question is what a piece is doing structurally — supporting a claim, anticipating an objection, illustrating a distinction, conceding a point before rejecting it.
Read the sentence
before
and
after
the cited material. Function is always relative to its neighbours, and the answer is usually visible in the transition into or out of it.
Answered by locating the author's evaluative language. Calibrate by degree, as
Passage Mapping
sets out, and remember that "neutral" or "expository" is a real and under-selected answer.
In the second paragraph, the word "plastic" is used to mean…

The passage's usage governs, not the dictionary's. Read the full sentence and the one before it, then substitute each candidate meaning and see which keeps the sentence coherent. The most common definition of the word is a deliberate lure. See
Phrase in Context
Which one of the following is most analogous to the relationship described in the passage?
Abstract the relationship, then match the abstraction — the same skill as
Parallel Reasoning and Parallel Flaw
. The choices are in unrelated domains on purpose, and matching on topic is always a mistake. See
Analogous Situation

Reading Comprehension distractors are usually accurate about half the passage. A choice that correctly describes the traditional view but attributes it to the author; a choice that captures ¶3's evidence but calls it the main point; a choice that gets the author's position right and overstates its strength.
The habit that catches these: read the
whole
choice, including the last few words. The exam hides the defect at the end more often than at the start, and readers who decide after the first clause miss it. See
Answer-Choice Elimination

items.text: Global and function questions are answered from the map; detail and inference from the text.
Detail questions are gettable and are missed through overconfidence — go back and read.
Inference standard: point at the supporting sentence, or eliminate.
Phrase-in-context is governed by the passage's usage; the common meaning is the lure.
Distractors are usually half right — read every choice to its end.

library.title: Reading Comprehension — Section Guide
library.summary: One 35-minute section, four passage sets, and a reading standard that rewards structure over recall — plus the time budget that makes it survivable.

spans.text: One scored 35-minute section: four passage sets, roughly 27 questions total. Three sets are a single passage of 450 to 550 words; one is a
comparative
set of two shorter passages on a common topic, which behaves differently enough to need its own treatment in
Comparative Passages

Subject matter rotates across four rough areas — law, humanities, social science, natural science — and none of it requires background knowledge. A passage on cephalopod neurology and a passage on legal formalism are the same task wearing different vocabulary.
Roughly 8 minutes 45 seconds per set. The split that works for most people:

rows.text: Return to the text for each one

spans.text: Two failure modes sit either side of that budget. Reading for
retention
— trying to hold the content in memory — takes six minutes and still fails, because the questions ask about things nobody remembers. Reading for
speed
— skimming in ninety seconds — means every question becomes a search through unmapped text.
The target is reading for
structure
: after one pass you should know what each paragraph does, where the author's own view sits, and where to look for anything else. See
Passage Mapping

items.text: What is this paragraph doing — introducing, complicating, conceding, refuting, illustrating?
Does the author endorse, reject, or withhold judgement, and how strongly? See
Whose view is this sentence? Passages routinely present two or three positions and the exam tests whether you tracked which is which.
What does the text license, and what does it merely fail to contradict? See

spans.text: Note what is missing: recall. You are allowed to look. The section is open-book, and treating it that way is the difference between a manageable set and an unmanageable one.

blocks.title: Reading for structure, in one pass

spans.text: A passage on the reception of a nineteenth-century legal treatise might map as:

lines: ¶1  Traditional view: the treatise was ignored in its time.
¶2  Evidence for the traditional view — sales figures, few reviews.
¶3  PIVOT. New archival work shows heavy citation in trial courts.
¶4  Author's position: influence was real but invisible to the
usual measures. Concedes the sales data is accurate.

spans.text: That map is four lines and about forty seconds of thought. It answers the main-point question outright, tells you the author's attitude, locates every detail question, and makes the "traditional view versus author's view" attribution questions trivial. Nothing about cephalopods or citation counts had to be memorised.
Passages are not ordered by difficulty and you are not required to take them in order. Two habits pay:

items.text: Start with the set you can read fastest
, if the difference is obvious in ten seconds of glancing. A dense abstract passage taken last is a passage you take with a clearer sense of your remaining time.
Never abandon a set you have already read.
The reading is the expensive part; the questions are comparatively cheap. Leaving a mapped passage to start an unmapped one is the worst possible trade. See

spans.text: The single most expensive habit in this section is answering a detail or inference question from what you remember reading. Memory reconstructs plausibly and the exam's wrong answers are built out of plausible reconstructions.
If a question is about what the passage says, go back and read the sentence. Every time. The map exists so that going back costs eight seconds instead of ninety.

items.text: One section, four sets, roughly 8:45 each — about 3:30 reading, 5:00 answering.
Read for structure and attribution, not for retention. The section is open-book.
A four-line paragraph map answers the global questions and locates the rest.
Take the easiest set first if it is obvious; never abandon a set you have already read.
Go back to the text for every question that is about the text.

library.title: Test-Day Conduct
library.summary: The controllable variables on exam day — environment, materials, break management, and the mid-exam decisions that cost the most points.

blocks.text: Rehearse the conditions, not just the content

spans.text: Whatever your administration format — remotely proctored at home or at a test centre — the single highest-return preparation is that exam day contains no novelty. Every practice exam in phase 4 of
Building a Study Plan That Survives Contact
should match the real thing on the variables you control: same start time, same chair, same scratch paper, same break length, no pausing between sections.

The reason is narrow and physical. Attention across four 35-minute sections is a trained capacity, and people who only ever drill single sections discover in section three that they have never held focus that long. That discovery costs more points than any question type.

A test taker averages 21 of 25 on drilled Logical Reasoning sections. On their first full four-section simulation they score 21, 20, and then 14. Nothing about the third section was harder. They had never once sat three in a row, and their accuracy fell off a cliff at the ninety-minute mark.
Four full simulations later the third-section number is 19. The fix was not method. It was endurance, and it is only trainable by simulating.

items.text: A cleared surface, a closed door, a phone in another room, and — for remote administration — a room that satisfies the proctoring rules
the day, checked once in advance rather than discovered at check-in.
Whatever your format permits, use exactly that in practice. If you get five sheets of scratch paper, practise with five, because running out mid-game is a scenario you want to have already met.

Eat something with slow carbohydrates ninety minutes before. Caffeine at your normal dose — exam day is the worst possible morning to change it. Hydrate to the point of comfort and no further; the break is short.
Be checked in early. Rushed check-in raises heart rate, and elevated arousal in section one is worth real points.

spans.text: There is one scheduled break, and it is the only structural reset the exam gives you. Use it deliberately:

items.text: Stand up and move. Circulation matters more than review.
Eat something small if you brought it.
try to recall questions from the first half. It changes nothing and it primes rumination.
Do not check the time obsessively; the proctor manages it.

spans.text: The most expensive habit on test day is grading yourself while the exam is still running. "That section went badly" is a judgement you cannot make accurately — every experienced test taker has felt a section go badly and scored well on it — and it is a judgement that damages the sections still to come.
The rule is:
the section is over when it is over.
No replaying, no estimating, no adjusting your plan for section four based on a feeling about section two. There is nothing to gain and a full section to lose.
Occasionally something genuinely breaks: a proctor interruption, a technical fault, a fire alarm. Two things matter.
First, follow the reporting procedure immediately and in writing. Complaints raised on the day carry weight that complaints raised a week later do not.
Second, and harder:
do not abandon the exam in your head.

A three-minute interruption is a three-minute interruption. It is not a ruined score unless you spend the following section deciding it was one. The decision to keep working at full effort after something goes wrong is worth more points than any technique in this library.

items.text: Rehearse the conditions: same start time, same materials, four sections with no pausing.
Endurance across three-plus sections is a separate trainable skill from accuracy on one.
Set up and verify the environment in advance; never discover a proctoring problem at check-in.
Use the break to move and eat, never to review the first half.
No mid-exam self-grading. Feelings about a section are uncorrelated with its score and they damage the next one.

library.title: The Argumentative Writing Method
library.summary: A five-paragraph structure that fits 35 minutes, how to make a concession that strengthens rather than weakens, and how to self-score against the rubric.

spans.text: Five paragraphs, each with one job. This is not the only workable shape, but it is the one that reliably fits 35 minutes and that a reader can follow at speed.

items.text: Name the position and the decision rule you are applying. Two to four sentences.
One reason, developed — fact from the scenario, the warrant connecting it to your position, and the consequence.
Same shape, different ground. If reason two is a restatement of reason one, cut it and develop reason one further.
The best argument against you, stated fairly, then answered.
Not a summary. One or two sentences on why, weighing everything, the decision still goes your way.

spans.text: The commonest weakness in a writing sample is assertion without connection. Every reason paragraph should contain three parts:

lines: Fact:        The scenario states the district exceeds the citywide
average for green space per resident.
Warrant:     Public investment should go where the deficiency is
greatest, not where the adequacy can be improved.
Consequence: So the marginal value of another park here is lower
than the marginal value of housing.

spans.text: The
warrant
is the part people skip, and it is the part that makes the paragraph an argument rather than an opinion. It is the same object as an assumption in
The Assumption Family
— the unstated principle linking evidence to conclusion — except here you are expected to state it. See
Warrant
A well-made concession makes your position stronger, because it shows you understood the cost and chose anyway. A badly-made one hands the essay away.

items.text: concede the fact, deny its weight.

"Green space genuinely improves health outcomes, and the park would deliver that. But the scenario describes a housing shortage as acute and green space as adequate, and severity governs when the two compete."
"The park might well be the better choice in some respects, and reasonable people could prefer it."
You have just written the other side's thesis into your own essay.

spans.text: The rule:
concede facts, never the criterion.
Grant that the other side's evidence is real, then explain why it does not decide the question. See
Concession and Scope

"The strongest case for the park is that green space is effectively irreversible once built over: a lot converted to housing will not become a park in this generation, while housing can be built on other sites. That asymmetry is real and it is the best argument against my position.

It does not carry the day here for two reasons. First, the scenario identifies no comparable site — the alternative is not 'housing later elsewhere' but 'housing later, unspecified'. Second, the irreversibility argument proves too much: applied consistently it would block any development on any vacant land, which is not a decision rule the city could actually adopt."

Note what this does. It states the objection at full strength, in the opponent's best terms. Then it answers on the record — with a fact from the scenario and a reductio. A reader finishes the paragraph more convinced, not less. See
Counterargument and Rebuttal
You will not get a score, so build the feedback loop yourself. After drafting, read your essay once against these questions:

rows.text: Is my position in the first three sentences?
The reader learns it in paragraph three
Does each reason have a stated warrant?
Did I state the objection at full strength?
A weak version I built to knock down
Did I concede a fact or the criterion?
Does every paragraph do one job?
Two arguments tangled in one paragraph
Would a reader know my decision rule?
Reasons stacked with no weighing principle

spans.text: Doing this on three practice essays is worth more than writing ten unreviewed ones — the same logic as
Blind Review

Length is not scored, and padding is visible. Repeating the thesis in different words, listing considerations you do not develop, and writing a summary conclusion that adds nothing all cost credibility with a reader who has seen thousands of these.
A tight 450-word essay that argues one position well reads better than an 800-word essay that covers more ground shallowly.

items.text: Five paragraphs: thesis with a decision rule, two developed reasons, counterargument and response, close.
Every reason needs fact, warrant, and consequence — the warrant is the part people skip.
Concede facts, never the criterion. State the objection at its strongest.
Self-score against a fixed checklist; three reviewed essays beat ten unreviewed.
Length earns nothing. Padding is visible and costs credibility.

library.title: Argumentative Writing — Section Guide
library.summary: The unscored-but-read writing sample — what the prompt gives you, what readers look for, and why a clear defensible position beats a balanced one.

blocks.text: What it is and why it matters

spans.text: LSAT Argumentative Writing is completed separately from the multiple-choice exam, on your own computer, under proctoring. It is
not scored numerically
and does not affect your 120–180 result. It is sent to every school you apply to, unedited, and your file is incomplete until you submit it.

That combination — unscored but read, and blocking — is why it gets neglected and why neglecting it is a mistake. Admissions readers use it as a writing sample that they know you produced alone, under time, without editing help. It is the one piece of your application whose authorship is certain.
A prompt presents a decision with two defensible positions, a short scenario, and several stated
perspectives
or criteria bearing on the choice. There is no correct answer. Both positions are supportable, and the prompt is constructed so that each has real costs.

lines: Scenario:   A city must choose between two uses for a vacant lot.
Position A: A public park.
Position B: Mixed-income housing.
Perspectives: housing shortage severity; existing green space
per resident; construction timeline; maintenance cost.

spans.text: You have a short pre-writing period and then 35 minutes to draft. Nothing is scored for length, and nobody is counting words.

blocks.text: What readers are actually looking for

items.text: A position, stated early and held.
The prompt asks you to choose. An essay that surveys both sides and declines to decide has not done the task. See
Not assertion — argument. Each reason should tie a fact from the scenario to your position through a stated warrant. See
Honest engagement with the other side.
The strongest essays name the best argument
their position and answer it. See
Claims you can defend in 35 minutes, qualified where they need qualifying. See
Paragraphs that each do one job. See

spans.text: Not on the list: vocabulary, sentence variety, rhetorical flourish, or outside knowledge. Nothing you know about urban planning helps; everything the prompt gave you does.
Surveying (weak opening):
"There are strong arguments on both sides of this difficult question. A park would provide green space, while housing would address a real need. Both considerations deserve weight."
Two sentences in and the reader knows nothing about what you think.
Committing (strong opening):

"The city should build the housing. The park's benefits are real but incremental — the district already exceeds the citywide average for green space per resident — while the housing addresses a shortage the scenario describes as acute. When one option addresses a severe deficiency and the other improves an existing adequacy, the severe deficiency governs."

The position is stated, the criteria are engaged, and a decision rule is offered that the rest of the essay can apply. That last move — supplying the principle by which you weighed the options — is what separates a strong sample from a competent one.

rows.text: Read the perspectives, pick a side, list your two strongest reasons and the strongest objection
Draft: thesis, reason, reason, counterargument and response, close
Read once for clarity and for sentences that say less than you meant

spans.text: Planning is not optional overhead. Five minutes of structure produces a better essay than five extra minutes of drafting, because the failure mode here is not running short — it is an essay that wanders.
Pick the position you can
argue better
, not the one you agree with. They are frequently different, and the prompt is designed so that both are defensible.
If one side has more support in the stated perspectives, take that side even if your instinct runs the other way. Nobody is reading this to learn your views on municipal land use.

items.text: Unscored, but sent to every school and required for a complete file.
Take a position in the first two sentences and hold it.
Argue from the stated perspectives; outside knowledge earns nothing.
Name the strongest objection and answer it — surveying both sides without deciding fails the task.
Plan for five minutes. The failure mode is wandering, not running short.

strategies.name: Abstract the form
strategies.summary: Strip the content and keep the skeleton: quantifiers, direction, validity. Match skeletons, never topics.

strategies.name: Apply the new condition
strategies.summary: Write the question's 'if' onto a fresh copy of the board and chain the inferences it forces. Answer from the mini-board, not from memory.

strategies.name: Attack or defend the link
strategies.summary: The premises are given as true. Strengthen or weaken the inference from them to the conclusion, never the premises themselves.

strategies.name: Bridge the terms
strategies.summary: Build the conditional that carries the premise term to the conclusion term. The answer that guarantees the conclusion is the bridge, stated in the right direction.

strategies.name: Build the board first
strategies.summary: Set up the slots, symbolise every rule, and make the up-front deductions before touching a question. Time spent here is repaid on every question after.

strategies.name: Calibrate the tone
strategies.summary: Match the hedging in the author's own words. 'Qualified approval' and 'unqualified enthusiasm' differ by exactly the words the passage used.

strategies.name: Chain the contrapositives
strategies.summary: Every membership rule has a contrapositive; write them all and follow the chain from the given element. The chain is the deduction.

strategies.name: Check both directions
strategies.summary: A substitute rule must forbid everything the original forbade and permit everything it permitted. Test each choice in both directions.

strategies.name: Check both passages
strategies.summary: A comparative answer must be supportable from each passage. Confirm it against both texts, not just the one that comes to mind.

strategies.name: Let context fix the meaning
strategies.summary: Reread the sentence before and after the quoted phrase. The author's contrast pins the local sense, and the dictionary sense is the trap.

strategies.name: Diagram the conditionals
strategies.summary: Symbolise every if-then, take its contrapositive, and chain them. Converse and inverse readings are the distractors, and the diagram makes them visible.

strategies.name: Enumerate the distributions
strategies.summary: List every legal split of counts across the groups before placing anyone. The list is the whole answer to a numeric question.

strategies.name: Find the conclusion first
strategies.summary: Locate the claim everything else is offered to support, then the support. Every LR task is defined relative to that conclusion.

strategies.name: Hunt for a counterexample
strategies.summary: For a global must-be-true, a choice that fails in even one valid arrangement is out. Use earlier acceptable arrangements as ready-made counterexamples.

strategies.name: Name the gap
strategies.summary: Write the premise terms and the conclusion terms side by side. The new term in the conclusion is where the argument leaps, and where the answer lives.

strategies.name: Locate, then verify
strategies.summary: Find the lines the question points at and match the choice against them word for word. Passage vocabulary recombined into an unstated claim is the standard distractor.

strategies.name: Map the passage
strategies.summary: Note each paragraph's job and the author's stance as you read. Global questions are answered from the map, not from rereading.

strategies.name: Name the flaw in your own words
strategies.summary: Before reading the choices, say what went wrong between premise and conclusion. Then find the choice that says the same thing in the test's abstract vocabulary.

strategies.name: Negation test
strategies.summary: Negate a candidate answer. If the argument falls apart without it, it was necessary; if the argument survives, it was not.

strategies.name: Pre-phrase the answer
strategies.summary: Say what the right answer must do before reading a single choice, so the choices are checked against your prediction rather than each other.

strategies.name: Keep both facts true
strategies.summary: The credited answer lets both surprising findings stand at once. Anything that denies one side or explains only one side is a distractor.

strategies.name: Role, not content
strategies.summary: Ask why the author put the reference there, not what it says. The answer names its argumentative job: illustrate, concede, rebut, qualify.

strategies.name: Rule-by-rule elimination
strategies.summary: Take one rule at a time and strike every choice that breaks it. Four wrong answers each violate a different rule, so you never have to build anything.

strategies.name: Stay inside the text
strategies.summary: An inference must be provable from what is written. Prefer the most modest choice; a choice that needs outside knowledge or a stronger word than the text used is wrong.

strategies.name: Test every condition
strategies.summary: Split the principle into its trigger conditions and check each choice against all of them. A scenario that meets most of the conditions meets none of the principle.

strategies.name: Track both dimensions
strategies.summary: In a hybrid game every inference must be checked against order and group together. A deduction that ignores one dimension is a guess.

strategies.name: Two-speaker test
strategies.summary: For a point at issue, both speakers must address the claim and take opposite sides. One silent speaker or two speakers who agree fails the test.

strategies.name: Variance test
strategies.summary: Answer the candidate question both ways. If one answer strengthens and the other weakens, the question is useful; if the argument is untouched either way, it is not.

strategies.name: Witness and contradiction
strategies.summary: Prove the credited number with one arrangement that achieves it, then show one more (or one fewer) breaks a rule. Both halves are required.

traps.name: Achievable in isolation
traps.summary: A count or placement that works on its own but collides with another rule once the rest of the board is filled.

traps.name: Concession mistaken for conclusion
traps.summary: Picks the clause the author granted to the other side, or a premise sitting behind 'since', as the main conclusion.

traps.name: Dictionary sense
traps.summary: The ordinary meaning of the quoted phrase rather than the meaning the author's contrast fixed for it.

traps.name: A flaw the argument did not commit
traps.summary: Names a real, well-known error (ad hominem, sampling, circularity) that this particular argument never made.

traps.name: Half the paradox
traps.summary: Explains why one finding happened without saying why the other did too, or simply denies one of them.

traps.name: Intensity overshoot
traps.summary: Right direction, wrong strength: 'hostile' for 'skeptical', 'unqualified' for 'cautious'.

traps.name: Equivalent in one direction only
traps.summary: A substitute rule that permits nothing new but forbids something old, or the reverse. Equivalence needs both.

traps.name: Supported by one passage only
traps.summary: True of Passage A or Passage B alone, offered as a claim about both, or attributes one author's view to the other.

traps.name: The opposite answer
traps.summary: Does the reverse of what the stem asked: a weakener on a strengthen question, a sufficient condition on a necessary one.

traps.name: Out of scope
traps.summary: Introduces a term, party or concern the stimulus never addresses. Plausible in the world, irrelevant to the argument.

traps.name: Polarity flip
traps.summary: The right topic with the wrong sign: approval read as criticism, or the author's opponent's view read as the author's.

traps.name: Premise booster
traps.summary: Restates or shores up a premise instead of bridging premise to conclusion. The premises were already granted.

traps.name: Quantifier swap
traps.summary: 'Most' where the text said 'some', 'all' where it said 'most'. A single quantifier word changes what follows.

traps.name: Reversed conditional
traps.summary: The converse or inverse of a rule: 'if Q then P' offered for 'if P then Q'. Only the contrapositive is equivalent.

traps.name: Same topic, different structure
traps.summary: Matches the stimulus on subject matter and diverges on form. Parallel and analogy questions are decided on form alone.

traps.name: Sample size red herring
traps.summary: Complains the sample was small when the real problem is how it was selected. Size is rarely the tested defect.

traps.name: Too narrow
traps.summary: True of one paragraph or one premise, but not of the whole argument or passage the stem asked about.

traps.name: Too strong
traps.summary: Says 'all', 'never', 'proves' where the text only said 'some', 'usually', 'suggests'. Extra strength is extra claims you cannot support.

traps.name: True of most boards
traps.summary: Holds in most valid arrangements but not all. A single counterexample arrangement kills a must-be-true answer.

traps.name: True of the argument, but not a defect
traps.summary: Accurately describes something the argument did, without that thing being a mistake.

traps.name: Answered a different question
traps.summary: A could-be-true offered where must-be-true was asked, or the EXCEPT overlooked so four right answers look wrong.

traps.name: Wrong term
traps.summary: Correctly alleges a shift in meaning, but in a term the argument used consistently.

traps.summary: Explains why one finding happened without saying why the other did too, or simply denies one of them.

traps.name: Out of scope
traps.summary: Introduces a term, party or concern the stimulus never addresses. Plausible in the world, irrelevant to the argument.

items.name: Role of a Claim
cues: The claim that ... plays which one of the following roles in the argument?
items.task: Say what job the quoted claim does: premise, intermediate conclusion, main conclusion, or concession.

strategies.name: Find the conclusion first
strategies.summary: Locate the claim everything else is offered to support, then the support. Every LR task is defined relative to that conclusion.

strategies.name: Abstract the form
strategies.summary: Strip the content and keep the skeleton: quantifiers, direction, validity. Match skeletons, never topics.

method: Find the main conclusion first; every other role is defined relative to it.
Ask of the quoted claim: is it supported by something, and does it support something?
Supported and supporting means intermediate conclusion; supporting only means premise.
The credited answer names the role abstractly; choices that describe content instead of role are decoys.

traps.name: Concession mistaken for conclusion
traps.summary: Picks the clause the author granted to the other side, or a premise sitting behind 'since', as the main conclusion.

traps.name: Too narrow
traps.summary: True of one paragraph or one premise, but not of the whole argument or passage the stem asked about.

items.name: Unrepresentative Sample Flaw
cues: The reasoning is flawed because it
items.task: The group observed was selected in a way that makes it unlike the population concluded about.

strategies.name: Name the flaw in your own words
strategies.summary: Before reading the choices, say what went wrong between premise and conclusion. Then find the choice that says the same thing in the test's abstract vocabulary.

strategies.name: Name the gap
strategies.summary: Write the premise terms and the conclusion terms side by side. The new term in the conclusion is where the argument leaps, and where the answer lives.

method: Find the group observed and the population the conclusion is about.
Ask how the group was gathered: self-selection, survivorship, convenience.
Name the mismatch between how it was gathered and who it is meant to represent.
Do not reach for 'too small'; the tested defect is selection, and size is the planted wrong answer.

traps.name: Sample size red herring
traps.summary: Complains the sample was small when the real problem is how it was selected. Size is rarely the tested defect.

traps.name: A flaw the argument did not commit
traps.summary: Names a real, well-known error (ad hominem, sampling, circularity) that this particular argument never made.

items.name: Strengthen
cues: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
items.task: Pick the new fact that makes the conclusion more likely to follow from the premises.

strategies.name: Find the conclusion first
strategies.summary: Locate the claim everything else is offered to support, then the support. Every LR task is defined relative to that conclusion.

strategies.name: Attack or defend the link
strategies.summary: The premises are given as true. Strengthen or weaken the inference from them to the conclusion, never the premises themselves.

strategies.name: Pre-phrase the answer
strategies.summary: Say what the right answer must do before reading a single choice, so the choices are checked against your prediction rather than each other.

method: Find the conclusion and the kind of support (causal, sample, analogy).
Ask what would rule out the obvious alternative explanation or confirm the mechanism.
Pick the choice that does that; treat 'if true' as licence to accept it.
Ignore choices about cost, popularity or authority; they do not touch the inference.

traps.name: The opposite answer
traps.summary: Does the reverse of what the stem asked: a weakener on a strengthen question, a sufficient condition on a necessary one.

traps.name: Out of scope
traps.summary: Introduces a term, party or concern the stimulus never addresses. Plausible in the world, irrelevant to the argument.

traps.name: Premise booster
traps.summary: Restates or shores up a premise instead of bridging premise to conclusion. The premises were already granted.

items.name: Sufficient Assumption
cues: Which one of the following, if assumed, allows the conclusion above to be properly drawn?
The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
items.task: Find the claim that, added to the premises, guarantees the conclusion.

strategies.name: Name the gap
strategies.summary: Write the premise terms and the conclusion terms side by side. The new term in the conclusion is where the argument leaps, and where the answer lives.

strategies.name: Bridge the terms
strategies.summary: Build the conditional that carries the premise term to the conclusion term. The answer that guarantees the conclusion is the bridge, stated in the right direction.

strategies.name: Diagram the conditionals
strategies.summary: Symbolise every if-then, take its contrapositive, and chain them. Converse and inverse readings are the distractors, and the diagram makes them visible.

method: Diagram the premises and the conclusion; note the term the premises reach and the term the conclusion needs.
Write the bridge: if (premise term) then (conclusion term).
Choose the choice that states that bridge, or something stronger.
A bridge in the other direction, or between the wrong terms, is the usual trap.

traps.name: Reversed conditional
traps.summary: The converse or inverse of a rule: 'if Q then P' offered for 'if P then Q'. Only the contrapositive is equivalent.

items.name: Weaken
cues: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
items.task: Pick the new fact that makes the conclusion less likely to follow from the premises.

strategies.name: Find the conclusion first
strategies.summary: Locate the claim everything else is offered to support, then the support. Every LR task is defined relative to that conclusion.

strategies.name: Attack or defend the link

strategies.name: Pre-phrase the answer
strategies.summary: Say what the right answer must do before reading a single choice, so the choices are checked against your prediction rather than each other.

method: Find the conclusion and the inference it rests on.
Predict the attack: a confound, reverse causation, a disanalogy, a bad sample.
Choose the choice that supplies it; do not reward a choice that merely denies a premise.
A choice that restates the conclusion, or attacks an irrelevance, is a decoy.

items.name: Analogous Situation
cues: ... is most analogous to which one of the following?
Which one of the following would best illustrate the passage's claim that
items.task: Find the scenario that shares the structure of the situation described, in an unrelated domain.

strategies.name: Abstract the form
strategies.summary: Strip the content and keep the skeleton: quantifiers, direction, validity. Match skeletons, never topics.

strategies.name: Map the passage
strategies.summary: Note each paragraph's job and the author's stance as you read. Global questions are answered from the map, not from rereading.

method: Reduce the passage situation to a relationship skeleton: who depends on whom for what.
Discard the subject matter entirely.
Match each choice's skeleton to yours.
The choice from the passage's own domain that matches topic and not structure is planted.

traps.name: Same topic, different structure
traps.summary: Matches the stimulus on subject matter and diverges on form. Parallel and analogy questions are decided on form alone.

traps.name: Too narrow
traps.summary: True of one paragraph or one premise, but not of the whole argument or passage the stem asked about.

items.name: Author's Attitude / Tone
cues: The author's attitude toward X is best described as
The author's assessment of X is best characterized as
items.task: Name the author's stance toward a specific target, calibrated to the passage's hedging.

strategies.name: Calibrate the tone
strategies.summary: Match the hedging in the author's own words. 'Qualified approval' and 'unqualified enthusiasm' differ by exactly the words the passage used.

strategies.name: Locate, then verify
strategies.summary: Find the lines the question points at and match the choice against them word for word. Passage vocabulary recombined into an unstated claim is the standard distractor.

method: Find every evaluative word the author uses about the target.
Decide the direction (approves, doubts) and the strength (cautious, wholehearted).
Pick the choice matching both direction and strength.
Polarity flips and intensity overshoots are the two families of wrong answer.

traps.name: Polarity flip
traps.summary: The right topic with the wrong sign: approval read as criticism, or the author's opponent's view read as the author's.

traps.name: Intensity overshoot
traps.summary: Right direction, wrong strength: 'hostile' for 'skeptical', 'unqualified' for 'cautious'.

items.name: Comparative Passages Relationship
cues: Both passages are committed to which one of the following?
The author of Passage A and the author of Passage B would be most likely to disagree about whether
Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?
items.task: Describe the relationship between the two texts: what both hold, where they part, or how one's approach differs.

strategies.name: Check both passages
strategies.summary: A comparative answer must be supportable from each passage. Confirm it against both texts, not just the one that comes to mind.

strategies.name: Map the passage
strategies.summary: Note each paragraph's job and the author's stance as you read. Global questions are answered from the map, not from rereading.

method: Before the questions, write one line each: what A argues, what B argues, and the point where they meet.
For each choice, test it against A, then separately against B.
The credited answer survives both tests.
A choice that one passage supports and the other never addresses is the standard distractor.

traps.name: Supported by one passage only
traps.summary: True of Passage A or Passage B alone, offered as a claim about both, or attributes one author's view to the other.

traps.name: Polarity flip
traps.summary: The right topic with the wrong sign: approval read as criticism, or the author's opponent's view read as the author's.

items.name: Explicit Detail
cues: According to the passage, ...
items.task: Find the fact the passage states and match the choice that paraphrases it.

strategies.name: Locate, then verify
strategies.summary: Find the lines the question points at and match the choice against them word for word. Passage vocabulary recombined into an unstated claim is the standard distractor.

method: Use the stem's keywords to find the line.
Read the sentence in full, including any qualifier.
Match the choice against the sentence, term for term.
Passage vocabulary recombined into an unstated claim, or the right fact about the wrong entity, is the trap.

traps.summary: Introduces a term, party or concern the stimulus never addresses. Plausible in the world, irrelevant to the argument.

traps.name: Too strong
traps.summary: Says 'all', 'never', 'proves' where the text only said 'some', 'usually', 'suggests'. Extra strength is extra claims you cannot support.

traps.name: Polarity flip

The primary function of the fourth paragraph is to
The discussion of X functions primarily to
items.task: Say why the author included the reference: the job it does for the argument.

strategies.name: Role, not content
strategies.summary: Ask why the author put the reference there, not what it says. The answer names its argumentative job: illustrate, concede, rebut, qualify.

strategies.name: Map the passage
strategies.summary: Note each paragraph's job and the author's stance as you read. Global questions are answered from the map, not from rereading.

method: Find the reference and read the sentences around it.
Ask what claim it serves: illustrating, conceding, rebutting, qualifying.
Pick the choice naming that role.
A choice that describes what the reference says, or assigns a role to a claim the passage never makes, is wrong.

items.name: Inference from the Passage
cues: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that
The passage most strongly supports which one of the following?
The author would be most likely to regard
items.task: Find the claim that follows from combining what the passage says, with nothing added.

strategies.name: Stay inside the text
strategies.summary: An inference must be provable from what is written. Prefer the most modest choice; a choice that needs outside knowledge or a stronger word than the text used is wrong.

strategies.name: Locate, then verify
strategies.summary: Find the lines the question points at and match the choice against them word for word. Passage vocabulary recombined into an unstated claim is the standard distractor.

method: Find the two or three sentences the question draws on.
Combine them; the inference is what they jointly imply.
Prefer the most modest choice they support.
Real-world plausibility is not support; a hedged passage claim restated as certainty is wrong.

traps.name: Too strong

method: From your paragraph map, say the passage's point in one sentence before reading choices.
Check that the credited answer covers the whole arc, not one paragraph.
Check it carries the author's attitude, not just the topic.
Strike choices that overstate, or that contradict a qualification the author made.

method: Write one verb per paragraph: introduces, criticises, qualifies, proposes.
Check each choice's sequence against your map, in order.

cues: In using the phrase "...", the author most likely means to convey that

items.task: Say what the quoted phrase means where it sits, which the author's contrast fixes.

strategies.name: Let context fix the meaning
strategies.summary: Reread the sentence before and after the quoted phrase. The author's contrast pins the local sense, and the dictionary sense is the trap.

strategies.name: Locate, then verify
strategies.summary: Find the lines the question points at and match the choice against them word for word. Passage vocabulary recombined into an unstated claim is the standard distractor.

method: Find the sentence containing the phrase and read the one before and after it.
Identify the contrast the author is drawing with it.
Restate the phrase in plain words that fit that contrast.
The ordinary dictionary sense, and a sense the phrase carries elsewhere, are the decoys.
